#4256. Tech Report: With Mortgage Rates Rising, Should You Hibernate Until Spring?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (773 w)

Tech Report: With Mortgage Rates Rising, Should You Hibernate Until Spring?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mortgage rates are back up this week, wiping out modest relief from a monthlong drop that began in mid-October.
  • Recent findings suggest that the average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage shot up 29 basis points to 7.28% APR in the week ending Nov.
  • A mortgage is a significant ol’ loan, so when rates go up, those fractions of a percentage point add up fast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mortgage rates are back up this week, wiping out modest relief from a monthlong drop that began in mid-October.

Recent findings suggest that the average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage shot up 29 basis points to 7.28% APR in the week ending Nov. 19, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

A mortgage is a significant ol’ loan, so when rates go up, those fractions of a percentage point add up fast. Say you’re borrowing $400,000 on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage. Compared with last week, your monthly principal and interest payment would be about $78 higher today.

Recent findings suggest that one bad week doesn't make a trend, but a jump like this can make putting your house hunt on hold until spring feel like a safer bet. So … is it?

Before deciding whether to buy a house now or wait, it helps to know what's pushing mortgage rates higher.

Right now, mortgage rates are still feeling the aftershocks from two major inflation reports last week. First, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) demonstrated consumer prices rose more than expected in October. Then, the Producer Price Index (PPI) showed wholesale inflation climbed 6.5% over the past year — its biggest annual increase in nearly four years.

While CPI shows how prices have changed, PPI can offer clues about what's coming next. Faced with higher costs, businesses may raise their own prices to compensate, keeping inflation elevated. Federal Reserve policymakers aren't expecting much relief anytime soon, either. According to meeting minutes released Nov. 18, they expect inflation to remain elevated above their 2% target for a while.

To cool rising prices, the Fed can raise the federal funds rate, which is the benchmark interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but lenders anticipate its decisions, so mortgage rates often move before the Fed acts. A rate hike is widely expected at the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting.

Even after a Fed rate hike, there’s no telling how promptly inflation will cool — or whether mortgage rates will follow. (Inflation is just one of many forces that affect mortgage rates, after all.) So if you do wait until spring to buy a house, don't do it just because you're betting on a cheaper mortgage.

If you're not in a rush to move, winter can be a good time to regroup. Fewer homes typically go up for sale from November through February, so waiting until spring could give you more options.

But new data from the National Association of Realtors suggests this year's slowdown goes beyond the usual seasonal lull. High mortgage rates and home prices are making it tough for many buyers to make the numbers work. For some buyers, waiting isn't a strategy — it's the only option.

Industry observers note that pending home sales, a measure of homes under contract, fell 16.7% in October compared with a year earlier, NAR reports. All four U.S. regions saw declines. At this rate, NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun warned that annual home sales could fall to their lowest level since the mid-1990s.

“Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans,” Yun said in a news release.

Whether you're waiting by choice or necessity, you can use the time to strengthen your finances. Paying down debt, strengthening your credit score or saving for a bigger down payment could help you qualify for a better mortgage deal.

Every little bit helps when today’s mortgage rates are this high.

Recent findings suggest that mortgage preapprovals typically expire after 60 to 90 days. If you're already preapproved, why not keep an eye on listings this winter? (Hey, I’m an optimist. All it takes is one house.).

Think like a seller for a second. If you're listing your house in the dead of winter, you're probably not doing it just for fun. You might have a deadline, and you’re probably more willing to negotiate. In the winter, buyers have less competition — and more room to negotiate a lower price, closing cost credits or repairs. Those savings on the sticker price might help offset today's higher borrowing costs.

Spring typically brings more homes for sale, but it also brings more buyers competing for them. And if mortgage rates end up dropping this spring, you won't be the only one coming out of hibernation.

While Nvidia stock is down 20% this year, driven by recent developments at the company, Broadcom has clocked paltry gains of just 2%. Nvidia may remain under pressure as investors and Wall Street await whether the company's incredible growth can hold up in the post-Jensen Huang era.

    In a recent development, broadcom, meanwhile, could have a solid 2027 due to terrific growth in the tech giant's AI semiconductor revenue. However, I think both Nvidia and Broadcom can be upstaged by another semiconductor stock in 2027 -- Cerebras Systems (CBRS +4.82%). Let's see why that may be the case.

    According to recent reports, cerebras Systems went public in May this year. The stock spiked 68% on the first day of trading following its initial public offering (IPO). However, the stock has slid significantly since then.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:56 AM ET 11/20/26.

    The stock's slide can be attributed to its expensive valuation when it went public, as well as concerns about the sustainability of the AI infrastructure build-out. However, Cerebras' growth and outlook clearly suggest that the market is underestimating its potential.

    According to recent reports, the manufacturer released third-quarter results on Nov. 12, reporting a 70% year-over-year increase in core revenue to $231 million. The figure was well ahead of the $214.7 million consensus estimate. Its adjusted loss of $0.12 per share was also lower than the Wall Street estimate of $0.14 per share. Importantly, Cerebras expects its business to take off substantially in 2027.

    Recent findings suggest that the organization designs and builds wafer-scale AI chips, which are dinner-plate-sized silicon wafers used as a stand-alone processor. Nvidia and Broadcom, for comparison, offer smaller chips such as graphics cards and custom processors, which need to be connected to other chips, storage, and compute memory in rack-scale systems via high-speed networking cables to run AI workloads.

    It has been revealed that cerebras' massive chip, on the other hand, integrates all the elements into a single platform. As a result, the manufacturer claims that its wafer-scale engine is significantly faster than traditional graphics cards. For instance, the company claimed in September last year that its CS-3 wafer-scale AI supercomputer is 21 times faster than Nvidia's DGX B200 Blackwell supercomputing system. What's more, Cerebras pointed out that the CS-3 costs 33% less and has equally lower power consumption.

    Sources indicate that it is worth noting that Cerebras doesn't just sell chips. It also operates a cloud service powered by its own chips, which allows customers to train AI models and run inference applications. The good news for investors is that Cerebras' business is poised for a significant lift-off next year.

    The manufacturer has contracts with major hyperscalers, such as Oracle, Microsoft, Amazon, and OpenAI, among others. Cerebras has added three upcoming hyperscalers to its clientele in the past six months. What's more, the company has also signed on neocloud customers who will offer inference services powered by Cerebras hardware in their data centers.

    Cerebras management points out that it is on track to exit 2026 with 10x the manufacturing capacity it had at the beginning of the year. The organization is also going to bring 700 megawatts (MW) of data center capacity online by late 2027 to bolster its cloud business. These factors explain why Cerebras expects its revenue to grow 3x in 2027.

    The tech giant expects $950 million in revenue this year, and the forecasts for the next couple of years suggest that Cerebras' business will grow significantly.

    CBRS Revenue Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts.

    Sources indicate that cerebras has a 12-month median price target of $207, implying a 120% jump from current levels, according to CNN. What's more, 13 of the 14 analysts covering Cerebras rate it as a buy. I won't be surprised to see Cerebras achieving such solid growth.

    Let's say Cerebras' revenue indeed reaches $3 billion in 2027, and it trades at 20 times sales then, lower than its current price-to-sales ratio of 23; its market cap will reach $60 billion. That's 137% higher than its current market cap. Of course, the U.S. tech sector has an average sales multiple of 6.3, and I am assuming that Cerebras will trade at a significant premium after a year. However, its stunning premium justifies the growth.

    On the other hand, Nvidia and Broadcom are expected to deliver gains of 66% and 48%, respectively, based on their 12-month median price targets. So, even analysts expect Cerebras stock to outpace its well-established peers.

    All this suggests that now is a good time for investors to buy Cerebras following its recent slide, as its outstanding growth prospects could help it outperform Nvidia and Broadcom over the coming year.

    Some Retirees May Pay State Income Tax on Social Security in These 8 States

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (484 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Death and taxes are usually mentioned in the same breath for a reason: They're unavoidable.
    • The good news is that 42 states plus Washington, D.C., don't tax Social Security benefits.
    • Here are the eight states that tax Social Security benefits:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Stefon Walters – Nov 20, 2026 at 6:55AM EST.

    Death and taxes are usually mentioned in the same breath for a reason: They're unavoidable. This goes for paychecks, investment gains, and even your Social Security benefits. Although you pay into Social Security through payroll taxes, benefits received in retirement are treated like other income and may be taxable.

    The good news is that 42 states plus Washington, D.C., don't tax Social Security benefits. The bad news is that leaves eight states that do. Let's look at which ones.

    Here are the eight states that tax Social Security benefits:.

    Who's subject to the tax and how much they're taxed varies widely by state. For example, in Connecticut, only single filers earning at least $75,000 and joint filers earning at least $100,000 are subject to the tax. If you earn above that, only up to 25% of your benefit is taxable.

    People earning below $86,410 (single filers) and $110,780 (joint filers) in Minnesota can subtract 100% of the federally taxable benefits, while Montana doesn't offer an exemption.

    In a recent development, if you're living in one of these states, check your state's specific rules. Many retirees in these states may find they're off the hook, even if the state has a tax in place.

    Industry observers note that even if you're lucky enough to be in one of the 42 states or D.C. that doesn't tax Social Security benefits, you're not automatically exempt from the federal tax on benefits. How much you pay (if anything) depends on your "combined income," which is a combination of the following:.

    If you're single and your combined income is under $25,000, you're off the hook with federal taxes. If it's between $25,000 and $34,000, up to 50% of your benefits could be taxed. If it's more than $34,000, up to 85% could be taxed.

    It has been revealed that if you're married and filing jointly with a combined income under $32,000, you're free from federal taxes. If it's between $32,000 and $44,000, up to 50% could be taxed. If it's more than $44,000, up to 85% could be taxed.

    Recent findings suggest that as an example, let's assume you're filing jointly, receive $40,000 in annual benefits, and have a combined income of $35,000. In this case, up to $20,000 of your benefits are eligible to be taxed. Once the IRS determines the exact taxable amount, it's added to your other forms of income and taxed at your normal income tax rate.

    #4252. Letter To The CEO: AI Decisions You Cannot Delegate

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (861 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    Letter To The CEO: AI Decisions You Cannot Delegate

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (861 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Madhu Shashanka is the Cofounder, Chief Scientist and CTO at Concentric AI and author of the forthcoming book, Coherence.
    • For thirty years, the fastest company usually won.
    • Building a workflow, analyzing a market, drafting a contract: work that once required scarce talent and real time now takes a goal and an instruction.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Madhu Shashanka is the Cofounder, Chief Scientist and CTO at Concentric AI and author of the forthcoming book, Coherence.

    For thirty years, the fastest company usually won. That era is ending, and most CEOs have not noticed.

    AI is making execution cheap. Building a workflow, analyzing a market, drafting a contract: work that once required scarce talent and real time now takes a goal and an instruction. When your team can build almost anything in an afternoon, and so can every competitor, speed stops being an advantage. Everyone has it.

    So what becomes scarce? Coherence: whether the growing crowd of autonomous systems inside your firm, and the people accountable for them, still pull in the same direction. It is the one advantage a competitor cannot buy, because no vendor sells it. Capability, by contrast, is commoditizing. Your rivals will soon run the same models you do, at the same price, so an AI strategy built on having better tools is built on eroding ground. What does not commoditize is the capability to deploy all that intelligence coherently: data trustworthy enough to reason over, calibrated knowledge of which systems to rely on for what, the judgment to know which complexity your company can absorb. You only build those over years, which is why a competitor cannot close the gap by switching vendors.

    Most companies are building the opposite. Execution got cheap, so everyone builds more. Sales stands up an agent, finance automates forecasting, operations wires up logistics. Each works. Each passes its own tests. On paper, the firm gets more automated every quarter, and quietly harder to run, because two agents now act on contradictory assumptions, decisions flow through systems no one fully understands and every team sharpens its own corner while the whole loses its shape. This is complexity debt, and you cannot see it on any dashboard. You feel it later, as the sense that nobody can quite explain why the organization behaves the way it does.

    Sources indicate that I learned the underlying lesson the humbling way, long before agents existed. Early in my career, I built a data visualization I was proud of: dense, elegant, the kind of thing that impresses engineers. Customers hated it. It was correct at the level I cared about and useless at the level that mattered. A system can be flawless at its task and still make the organization worse. Task-level success and enterprise value are different things, and most companies measure only the first, one agent at a time, across the whole enterprise.

    Sources indicate that this lands on your desk because the fix isn’t technical. Your Chief AI Officer can build the discipline. Only you can decide the company will live by it. Four acts are yours alone.

    Recent findings suggest that set the risk appetite. How much unreviewed autonomy the manufacturer will accept, and in which domains it will never let a system act without a human, is a statement about your institution’s identity, not a technical parameter. The organization calibrates to it whether you say it out loud or not. So say it out loud.

    Protect the function that can tell you no. Whatever coherence capability you build will, by design, sometimes block a business-unit head who wants to ship, a revenue line that wants to move and occasionally you. The organization learns whether that function is real not from the org chart but from what happens the first time its judgment constrains you. Accept a no you had the power to override, and you teach the firm that coherence is not ceremonial. Route around it, and you teach the opposite—whatever the documents say. This single act decides whether any of it survives contact with the organization.

    It has been revealed that hold the capital rule: build the judgment now, rent the plumbing later. The tools that monitor and permission autonomous systems are becoming cheap commodities you should buy. The judgment about what to deploy, decline and reverse is the asset, and it must be built inside your firm. Holding that line against the pressure to build bespoke versions of what the market will soon sell cheaply is capital allocation—your defining act.

    Reward the right thing. An organization optimizes the metrics its CEO asks about in reviews. Celebrate how many systems shipped, and you get deployment counts and the incoherence they generate. Ask whether the firm can still see what its systems are doing and still recover when one fails, and you get coherence, because you have signaled that is the real scorecard.

    According to recent reports, none of this asks the manufacturer to slow down. It asks the company to prove it can go fast without coming apart, a higher bar than speed and the only one now worth setting. The agentic era will make your enterprise into one of two things: an organization you could have designed, or one that assembled itself from local decisions nobody chose in full view. Which one you get is the decision with your name on it, and no one else’s.​.

    Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Micah Zimmerman – Nov 20, 2026 at 7:00AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Micron Technology ›.

    Sources indicate that colette Kress has had a whirlwind week. Last Thursday, she went from Nvidia's (NVDA -3.43%) longtime finance chief to its interim chief executive officer after CEO Jensen Huang abruptly resigned. On Nov. 18, after Nvidia posted results, she told CNBC something every memory investor should hear: "What we need in terms of chips, what we need in terms of advanced packaging or memory, all of that is also coming together.".

    Memory is Micron Technology's (MU -6.35%) whole world, and the Nvidia drama has helped drag Micron’s stock far below this year's high. That's why I'm circling Micron's next earnings report, due in December, on my calendar. Micron hasn't unveiled the exact day yet, but last year it reported its fiscal first-quarter results on Dec. 17.

    Recent findings suggest that the report will cover the first quarter of a year Micron's leaders have hyped for months. "As strong as fiscal 2026 was, we expect fiscal 2027 to be even better," CEO Sanjay Mehrotra mentioned in September, adding that supply and demand should be "much tighter in fiscal 2027 and 2028 than they were in 2026.".

    The bigger reason December matters is what comes after it. Micron has already locked in most of its 2027 supply of high bandwidth memory (HBM), the stacked chips that sit right beside artificial intelligence (AI) graphics processors, at significantly higher prices. Those prices "reset at the beginning of the calendar year," Micron President Manish Bhatia noted. That means the guidance Micron gives in December will be the first to bake in those new prices. That forecast matters more to me than the quarter itself.

    The quarter has a soft spot. Micron paid every employee a bigger bonus for 2026, and Chief Financial Officer Mark Murphy stated much of that cost hits now, calling fiscal Q1 "the floor for gross margins in fiscal 2027." A dip is expected, and I'd only worry if the outlook for the next quarter doesn't improve.

    According to recent reports, I also want to hear how Micron's newest chips are selling. Micron is in high-volume production of HBM4 chips built for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform, and Nvidia said that Vera Rubin systems have started shipping. Next up is a custom version co-designed with Nvidia, which Micron technology chief Scott DeBoer called "the first major custom HBM product out in the market.".

    It has been revealed that that closeness cuts both ways. If Nvidia's leadership shake-up slows its orders, Micron feels it fast. Micron also has the smallest market share of the three major HBM makers, and rivals SK Hynix (SKHY -2.53%) and Samsung (SSNLF +0.00%) are building huge latest factories in South Korea.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:52 AM ET 11/20/26.

    In a recent development, micron has spent the year locking customers into multiyear supply deals. It has signed 26, and customers have backed them with $32 billion in commitments, mostly cash deposits. Partners include General Motors (GM -0.23%) and Ford Motor Company (F +3.34%), and Micron struck a separate strategic deal with Claude maker Anthropic. "The AI revolution has permanently elevated the role of memory and storage solutions from the data center to the edge," noted Chief Business Officer Sumit Sadana. Newly introduced deals in December would tell me customers aren't flinching.

    Shareholders could get more, too. Starting Dec. 9, limits on buybacks tied to Micron's federal CHIPS Act funding ease up. "Over time, we expect to return 100% of our excess cash to shareholders," Murphy remarked. December's call should show how hard Micron plans to lean in.

    Then there are the factories, which is where I get a little nervous. In Taiwan, where most of Micron's DRAM came from in 2026, Micron has all but halted construction of a new memory plant amid a drawn-out labor dispute, according to Bloomberg.

    In a recent development, memory has always been a boom-and-bust business, and every new fabrication plant in the semiconductor industry brings the day when supply catches up to demand a little closer. For now, Mehrotra says, "We do not have line of sight to when supply and demand will return to balance.".

    If December highlights 2027 prices sticking, customers still signing, and Nvidia's turmoil staying inside Nvidia, I think Micron's rough autumn will look like a buying opportunity.

    This Oceanfront Hilton Resort in Florida Is Great for Groups

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1499 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that hilton is making a major play in South Florida with its Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort.
    • The resort caters primarily to business and group travelers (it’s attached to a massive events space), but it’s also a strong option for vacationers looking for some R&R.
    • It has been revealed that room rates typically run $300 to $600 a night, depending on the season, but you can also use Hilton Honors benefits to make your stay more affordable.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that hilton is making a major play in South Florida with its Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort. The massive 1,000-room property — which underwent an $80 million renovation before opening under the Signia Hilton brand in May 2026 — sits on the beach in Hollywood, Florida, just outside of Fort Lauderdale.

    The resort caters primarily to business and group travelers (it’s attached to a massive events space), but it’s also a strong option for vacationers looking for some R&R. The main downside: The location isn’t great if your trip primarily revolves around off-property excursions, dining and nightlife.

    It has been revealed that room rates typically run $300 to $600 a night, depending on the season, but you can also use Hilton Honors benefits to make your stay more affordable. There’s also a resort fee of $59 per night — but Hilton waives that when you book using Hilton points.

    Hilton covered the cost of my stay for two nights, but the opinions in this review are my own. Here’s what guests can expect at this oceanfront resort.

    Since the Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort is part of Hilton Honors, there are several ways to book a stay there.

    Recent findings suggest that if you’re using Hilton points, expect to pay 70,000 to 80,000 points a night when standard rooms are available. Hilton elite status — a benefit you can earn by holding any Hilton Honors credit card — gets you the fifth-night-free perk, where you stay for at least five nights but pay for four when booking with points.

    For example, if you were to stay five nights at 80,000 points a night, you’d pay 320,000 points total, bringing down your average nightly rate to 64,000 points.

    According to recent reports, you can also book using Hilton’s generous free night certificates, which can be used at almost any property in the portfolio. If you hold the Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card, you automatically get a certificate each year. It’s also possible to earn certificates through reaching spending thresholds on the card and on the Hilton Honors American Express Surpass® Card. Terms apply.

    Recent findings suggest that make sure to check the cash rate against the points rate to make sure you’re getting good value from your redemption. NerdWallet values Hilton points at 0.4 cent apiece.

    For cash bookings of two nights or more, you might consider using The Hotel Collection via American Express’ travel portal for eligible cardholders. Eligible bookings come with benefits like a $100 property credit and other amenities subject to availability, including a room upgrade, early check-in and late checkout.

    Keep in mind that third-party bookings typically don’t earn Hilton points or count toward elite status qualification.

    It’s hard to miss the Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort, with its signature H-shaped facade and sleek white-and-glass exterior.

    Stepping into the hotel, I was immediately struck by the lush greenery filling the entrance and indoor courtyard. The grand lobby has soaring glass ceilings, giving the space a greenhouse feel, although the strong air conditioning keeps you cool.

    Despite its massive size, it doesn’t have a sprawling layout, which I appreciated. Everything is close together, and you can walk from the check-in counter to any of the indoor restaurants in under a minute.

    Industry observers note that I stayed in an oceanfront suite with a balcony, which was spacious and had a fun beachy vibe. To get to the rooms, you’ll need to use either the north or south tower elevator banks.

    In the living room, there was a large sitting area featuring a TV, a couch, an accent chair and a four-person high-top table.

    Although I didn’t spend too much time on the balcony — the October balminess was a bit too much for me — I enjoyed stepping out each morning to admire the view.

    The bedroom had a king bed with extremely comfortable bedding and an oversized chair that was a great spot to relax and read a book by the window.

    The bathroom was spacious, featuring a shower and a separate tub (something every room has).

    Even the standard room I toured felt roomy. I liked that it shared similar elements with the suite, including the oversized lounge chair.

    This is what you’d normally get when booking a room at the cheapest points price.

    There are several dining venues on the property, ranging from a grab-and-go cafe to a high-end steakhouse. It is a luxury resort, so expect the prices to reflect that.

    For breakfast, you can head to Palmea Kitchen, which is also open for lunch. I had the breakfast buffet, which offered a nice spread of classics, from hot food items and pastries to cold cuts and smoked salmon.

    In a recent development, if you don’t have time for a sit-down breakfast, you can head next door to The Press, which offers made-to-order and grab-and-go food options throughout the day. You can also get smoothies, juices, snacks, pastries and other sweet treats.

    The Canteen is another grab-and-go option that also sells snacks, drinks, souvenirs and sundries, similar to a convenience store.

    It has been revealed that for lunch and dinner, try Solara. It doesn’t have a traditional restaurant feel, as it’s mostly an indoor-outdoor bar space. One side connects to the lobby, while the other side faces the Solara adults-only pool.

    It serves a lunch menu, as well as a substantial bar food menu that’s available late into the night.

    According to recent reports, you can also eat at Playa Beach Bar & Grill, a beachside restaurant serving Latin-inspired cuisine. I enjoyed spending a lazy lunch there and watching the waves crash onto the shore.

    For a fancy sit-down dinner, go to Diplomat Prime, the property’s steakhouse. We had a group dinner at the restaurant, and the meats were, of course, the highlight. But don’t sleep on the seafood, which was also delicious.

    Sources indicate that one of the best parts of the Dip, as it’s affectionately known, is its location right on the beach. Guests can access the stretch of beach directly adjacent to the property. But it’s not a private beach, so you might encounter crowds.

    I didn’t spend any time on the beach itself — it was extremely windy while I was there — but the hotel’s resort fee includes amenities like a beach lounge (umbrella not included), a daily one-hour kayak or paddleboard rental, and beachfront yoga classes.

    If you don’t want to get sand everywhere, you can head to one of the three pool options: the adults-only Solara pool, the family-friendly lagoon pool and the Verandah Social Club for those 21 and older (requires paid access).

    According to recent reports, the family-friendly lagoon spans the length of the property and runs beneath the Solara pool. It also has its own hot tub.

    I spent an afternoon in a cabana at the Verandah Social Club, which has some smaller plunge pools and a hot tub.

    I appreciated the attentive service from the staff there, who constantly checked on whether guests needed anything.

    If you’re looking for other ways to stay active, head to the two-story fitness center, featuring a variety of equipment like free weights, exercise bikes, a rowing machine and treadmills.

    Sources indicate that next door, you’ll find the spa and wellness center. I had a relaxing massage that incorporated hot stones and aromatherapy.

    The locker rooms come with a sauna and steam room, although I wished there were more amenities like a hot tub and cold plunge.

    One of the resort fee inclusions is complimentary high-intensity interval training workout classes at the gym across the street. I signed up for an early morning class. The instructor was friendly, and it was a great way to start my day.

    Other amenities include a complimentary one-hour e-bike rental each day, as well as a kids’ club with various activities (but drop-off fees apply).

    I had a fantastic stay at this resort, but I’d recommend it for a specific traveler.

    It has been revealed that if you’re planning to stay on-property your entire trip, it’s a great option. That’s probably why it’s such a popular convention hotel, since everything you need is easily accessible.

    I loved the hotel’s design, including the jungle-like atmosphere in the lobby, and I found the dining options to be tasty, albeit pricey.

    But if your trip revolves around visiting Miami attractions, you’ll likely want to stay closer to the action.

    #4243. Why Most Third-Party Risk Programs Are Taking The Wrong Measurements

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (890 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Most Third-Party Risk Programs Are Taking The Wrong Measurements

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Girish Redekar is Co-founder and CEO of Sprinto, building the future of trust for high-growth companies.
    • ​I have answered security questionnaires as a vendor and sent them out as a buyer.
    • The trouble starts when the questionnaire becomes the risk program instead of being one input to it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Girish Redekar is Co-founder and CEO of Sprinto, building the future of trust for high-growth companies.

    ​I have answered security questionnaires as a vendor and sent them out as a buyer. On both sides, they do something useful: They surface what you cannot learn about a firm from the outside.

    The trouble starts when the questionnaire becomes the risk program instead of being one input to it.

    A vendor tells you they enforce MFA, patch critical vulnerabilities within a defined SLA and encrypt customer data. All useful. But none of those answers tells you whether privileged access has drifted since. Or that the vendor shipped an AI feature last Tuesday, and your customer data now passes through a model provider you have never reviewed.

    Every one of those answers can still be accurate. The questionnaire tells you what the vendor’s controls were designed to do. Your risk program needs to know what is actually happening today.

    Measuring vendor risk only through questionnaires has a well-known flaw: The vendor grades themselves. But there are two other flaws that do more damage.

    The first is age. A questionnaire is like the fire safety certificate framed in a restaurant lobby: accurate on the day it was issued. If you review vendors once a year, that snapshot guides your decisions for the next 12 months.

    In a recent development, the second is that very different vendors often get pushed through versions of the same process. The payroll provider with salary data for your entire company and the tool your design team uses for designing mockups can end up answering much of the same questionnaire and landing in the same folder marked approved.

    Some teams respond by sending the questionnaire every quarter instead of every year. I understand the instinct, but it gets them the same snapshot four times as often. AI makes this even easier, with vendors using it to fill out questionnaires and buyers using it to grade them. The paperwork moves faster, but what changed after approval is still invisible.

    Imagine a vendor passes review in March. In August, your sales team connects it to the CRM, and it starts holding customer records. Nobody reviews the change because the vendor is already approved. In November, the vendor discloses a breach, and you find out your customer data was part of it.

    Recent findings suggest that the analyst who approved the vendor can show you a complete file. Her work ended at approval. The eight months after it fell between teams.

    According to recent reports, A questionnaire tells you what a vendor says should be true. You also need evidence of what is changing around that vendor. That is what I mean by exposure evidence.

    Most of that evidence comes from how the business runs after approval. A tool approved for marketing gets rolled out to sales and starts holding pipeline data. The vendor switches on an AI feature by default in a routine upgrade. Neither change passes back through procurement, and an external security score could miss both because nothing visible from the outside changed.

    Continuous monitoring is what makes those signals useful. It watches for changes that alter the risk you originally accepted: a broader permission, a new use case, more sensitive data or access that should have expired. It also tells you which changes need attention and which do not, so you are not sending every vendor back through the same review.

    All of it serves one decision: If this vendor came up for approval today, with what you now know, would you still approve it?

    A board member asks a simple question: If one of our vendors were breached tomorrow, how exposed are we?

    Industry observers note that you might refer to the approval status: Every critical vendor was reviewed this year, and every one passed. That is a true statement about last spring.

    A better answer sounds like this: Two vendors expanded into systems holding customer data this quarter, and both were re-reviewed. One switched on an AI feature that sends data to an outside model provider, so we reopened the assessment and restricted its use while we review the change. Here is what we are watching next quarter.

    The second answer takes three minutes and gives the board something to act on.

    The first one describes a folder.

    If I had to replace questionnaire completion rates with a single number, it would be the days between a change at a critical vendor and someone on your team knowing about it. On an annual review cycle, that can be months.

    In a recent development, you can start shrinking that number this week. List the 10 vendors that hold your customer data or touch production, and name one person who owns changes to each. Then ask that person what has changed at each vendor since it was last approved. If they have to email the vendor to find out, that gap is your answer.

    Sources indicate that the certificate in the lobby will keep saying the restaurant passed inspection. It won’t tell you someone stacked boxes in front of the fire exit last week. Your program should be measuring how swiftly you notice.​.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, with the exception of earnings season, few data dumps are more valuable to investors than the quarterly filing of Form 13Fs with regulators.
    • According to recent reports, billionaire David Tepper, who oversees nearly $7.6 billion in assets under management at Appaloosa, is among Wall Street's most revered fund managers -- and he was a busy bee in the third quarter.
    • According to recent reports, appaloosa's David Tepper was a busy bee in the third quarter.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Sean Williams – Nov 20, 2026 at 7:06AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Amazon ›.

    In a recent development, with the exception of earnings season, few data dumps are more valuable to investors than the quarterly filing of Form 13Fs with regulators. A 13F allows investors to track which stocks Wall Street's brightest and most successful money managers purchased and sold in the latest quarter (in this instance, during the third quarter).

    According to recent reports, billionaire David Tepper, who oversees nearly $7.6 billion in assets under management at Appaloosa, is among Wall Street's most revered fund managers -- and he was a busy bee in the third quarter. Tepper modestly pared down what had been his fund's top holding, dual-industry leader Amazon (AMZN -0.12%), and bulked up Appaloosa's stake in another foundational artificial intelligence (AI) stock, Micron Technology (MU -6.35%).

    According to recent reports, appaloosa's David Tepper was a busy bee in the third quarter. Image source: Getty Images.

    According to Appaloosa's newest 13F, its billionaire boss disposed of 525,000 shares of Amazon, reducing his fund's remaining stake to 4,475,000 shares. Nevertheless, it still accounts for roughly 15% of Appaloosa's invested assets.

    Industry observers note that tepper's modest selling may be due to simple profit-taking. Appaloosa has been a continuous shareholder of Amazon stock for more than seven years, with shares effectively tripling over that time.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:53 AM ET 11/20/26.

    Sources indicate that but it's also possible that Tepper is concerned about Amazon's aggressive capital expenditures (capex) tied to the AI infrastructure build-out. The firm logged a staggering free cash outflow of $33.4 billion during the September-ended quarter, with capex more than doubling from the comparable quarter in 2025. If fundamentals come back into focus, Amazon (and other hyperscalers) could take it on the chin.

    Recent findings suggest that however, for investors playing the long game, it's been business as usual for Amazon. In addition to dominating online retail sales, revenue growth in its higher-margin cloud infrastructure services segment, Amazon Web Services (AWS), is accelerating. The integration of generative AI and large language model solutions lifted AWS's year-over-year sales growth to 39% in the third quarter.

    In a recent development, whereas Appaloosa's billionaire chief reduced his fund's stake in Amazon by 10%, he scooped up another 275,000 shares of memory and storage solutions leader Micron Technology, increasing the position by 28% to 1,250,000 shares from the June-ended quarter and making it the upcoming No. 1 holding.

    The (likely) lure for David Tepper is Micron's foundational position in the AI data center build-out. The firm is a key provider of high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which is packaged with graphics processing units to transfer data at jaw-dropping speed.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:52 AM ET 11/20/26.

    Micron has benefited from two dynamics. Firstly, the overwhelming demand for HBM and solid-state drives has boosted its pricing power and enabled the company to lock in more than $100 billion in strategic customer agreements (SCAs) through 2030.

    Recent findings suggest that secondly, despite the best efforts of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM -2.81%), HBM supply shortages persist. Ongoing supply shortages are affording Micron exceptional pricing power and its highest-ever gross margin.

    According to recent reports, however, history has repeatedly shown that strong pricing power for commoditized tech products, such as memory, tends to be short-lived. While Micron's SCAs should be able to offset potential price weakness for the foreseeable future, historical factors point to earnings multiple compression and the possibility of an AI bubble-bursting event taking place.

    The stock market has been volatile lately due to a series of macroeconomic risk factors and concerns about valuations for the companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry that has been so central to the market's gains in recent years.

    According to recent reports, along those lines, some investors are worried that big wins for the Democratic Party in the recent U.S. midterm elections could impede data center buildouts, lead to the introduction of new regulations, and put some leading players in the AI space under greater scrutiny.

    Stocks could continue to face some bearish pressures in the near term, but investors shouldn't overreact to the possibility of political headwinds. In fact, history notes that the stock market typically enjoys strong performance in the year following midterm elections.

    According to recent reports, due in part to uncertainty connected to the implications of election results, the stock market has tended to see more volatility and produce weaker returns in years that play host to midterm elections. Conversely, the year of trading following midterm elections has tended to produce strong returns.

    Recent findings suggest that since 1950, the S&P 500 has delivered an average return of 15% in the year of trading following midterms. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq Composite has posted an average annual return of nearly 26% in post-midterm years since its founding in 1971. That kind of historical backdrop could suggest that now is a worthwhile time to put some investment dollars into the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ -0.60%) -- an exchange traded fund (ETF) that tracks the Nasdaq-100 index and includes the 100 largest non-financials companies on the Nasdaq exchange.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:56 AM ET 11/20/26.

    According to recent reports, on the other hand, it's key to keep in mind that past performance is no guarantee of future results. There are some unique dynamics on the table right now that could cause a divergence from typical post-midterm stock market trends next year.

    For starters, inflation has continued to run relatively hot -- and there's a fair chance that the Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will vote for an interest rate increase this year and at least one additional rate hike next year. Higher interest rates help to combat inflation, but they also create a less favorable backdrop for the stock market -- and growth stocks in particular. Adding additional macroeconomic pressures, bond yields have remained stubbornly high.

    In a recent development, massive valuation gains for leading AI companies including Nvidia, Alphabet, and Microsoft in recent years also mean that indexes including the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite have become increasingly concentrated in recent years. This means that an investment in the Invesco QQQ Trust would likely face strong valuation pressures if sentiment surrounding top AI names shifts in a more bearish direction.

    In summary, the historical trend suggests that the Nasdaq Composite, the Nasdaq 100, and the Invesco QQQ Trust should see strong returns in the year to come -- but investors also shouldn't treat that outcome as a given.

    #4237. Industry News: Your Best Suppliers Are Losing Bookings They Deserve To Win

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (844 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Your Best Suppliers Are Losing Bookings They Deserve To Win

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Abhinav Sinha is Co-founder and CEO of ZentrumHub, a unified hotel API platform serving 90+ OTAs globally.
    • Earlier this year, my team audited the supplier routing of a midsize online travel agency.
    • When we asked why the order looked the way it did, we got the most honest answer in hotel distribution: That’s the order the contracts were signed in.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Abhinav Sinha is Co-founder and CEO of ZentrumHub, a unified hotel API platform serving 90+ OTAs globally.

    Earlier this year, my team audited the supplier routing of a midsize online travel agency. One wholesaler was confirming nearly every booking it received for hotels in Japan. It had deep direct contracts in the market, clean rates and almost no relocations. It sat fourth in the call sequence. Two of the suppliers ahead of it were failing roughly one booking in 10 on the same properties.

    When we asked why the order looked the way it did, we got the most honest answer in hotel distribution: That’s the order the contracts were signed in.

    For a decade, our industry has repeated the same line: Supplier loyalty is dead, wholesale inventory is a commodity and the only lever left is margin. I think the diagnosis is wrong. Loyalty isn’t dead. It’s invisible. Most distribution systems were never built to see which supplier is actually performing, so they have no way to reward it.

    The commodity story collapses the moment you look at supplier behavior property by property. Wholesalers and aggregators invest in very specific strengths—direct contracts in a handful of markets, rate accuracy on particular chains, confirmation reliability, clean cancellation handling, content depth. These investments are real and expensive.

    In a recent development, the channel they flow through isn’t a backwater, either. Expedia Group reported B2B gross bookings up 21% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, well ahead of its consumer business, marking its 20th consecutive quarter of double-digit B2B growth. The money moving through B2B hotel distribution keeps compounding. The sophistication with which buyers choose among suppliers for any single booking has barely moved.

    Recent findings suggest that at most booking platforms I’ve seen, supplier selection is static. A preference order is written when contracts are signed. It reflects commercial politics, integration chronology and whoever had the best rates during the pilot, and it’s rarely revisited.

    According to recent reports, from then on, every search walks the same waterfall. The supplier that’s genuinely best for this hotel, on these dates, for this traveler, often isn’t asked at all or is asked last after caches and timeouts have already shaped the answer.

    Static routing also protects the wrong suppliers. When buyers can’t distinguish disciplined suppliers from leaky ones, the whole category gets judged together. The mid-year World Parity Monitor found at least one online travel agency undercutting the hotel’s own website in 75% of searches, and a recurring driver it identifies is wholesale rates resold with unauthorized discounts.

    A supplier that keeps its rates clean ends up subsidizing the reputational damage caused by one that doesn’t because the routing layer can’t tell them apart. With performance invisible, the only lever anyone can pull is margin. The race to the bottom is a routing artifact.

    It has been revealed that the alternative is to route every request on observed performance for that property and market—availability accuracy, booking confirmation rate, cancellation and relocation rates, content quality and net price after failure costs rather than headline price. Each of these is measurable per supplier, per property, from data that platforms already generate.

    According to recent reports, when selection runs on that data, the supplier who invested in Japan wins Japan. The incentives flip. Investment becomes visible, visibility gets rewarded and suppliers start competing on reliability as well as price. In the migrations I’ve been close to, the first effect is usually not cheaper rooms but fewer failed bookings, which turns out to be worth more.

    If you run distribution or supply at a travel platform, four moves matter most in my experience:.

    1. Measure per property, not per contract. Portfolio averages hide everything important.

    It has been revealed that 2. Price in failure since a rate that’s 2% cheaper but fails far more often isn’t cheaper once you count rebooking costs and customer damage.

    In a recent development, 3. Treat routing as a living system, reviewed continuously rather than at contract renewal.

    4. Share scorecards with your suppliers. The ones worth keeping will improve whatever they can finally see.

    Industry observers note that if you’re a supplier, ask every buyer one question: How do you decide which of us gets the booking? If the answer is contract order, then a configuration file is neutralizing the market strengths you spent years building.

    According to recent reports, I argued in July that this industry still prices shopping as if it were scarce. Allocation is the same story one layer down. My bet is that within two years, “how does your routing decide?” becomes a standard question in supplier negotiations ahead of another round of margin shaving. The suppliers that ask it, and the platforms that can answer it with data, will take share from everyone still routing by paperwork.

    According to recent reports, loyalty was never dead. We just never gave it a scoreboard.​.

    10 stocks we like better than Rocket Lab ›.

    According to recent reports, rocket Lab (RKLB -0.77%) stock "missed earnings" last week, reporting losses nearly twice as bad as Wall Street had predicted. And then the stock shot up -- and kept going up. By the close of trading last Friday, Rocket Lab stock was up nearly 16% from where it began the week.

    In a recent development, heading into the earnings report, analysts forecast Rocket Lab would lose $0.07 per share on sales of $257.2 million. Actual losses were $0.12 per share, however. Rocket Lab reported $268 million in Q3 sales, beating on that metric -- and it looks like there may be more gains in store.

    Sources indicate that revenue hit a upcoming quarterly record, rising 73% year over year to $268 million. Backlog of work to be done, however (i.e., future revenue), grew by nearly 6x that number -- $1.2 billion -- bringing the total backlog to $3.6 billion.

    As fast as Rocket Lab grew in Q3, this massive backlog implies it's going to grow even faster in the future.

    Also key is CEO Sir Peter Beck's observation that the firm signed $470 million in Space Systems contracts and "nearly $1 billion" in fresh launch contracts in the quarter.

    It has been revealed that why is this crucial? Consider that, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence, Rocket Lab's Launch Services division earned 43% gross profit margins over the last 12 months, while Space Systems earned closer to 33.6%. That's nearly a 10-percentage-point difference in profitability between Rocket Lab's two main divisions, with the advantage currently going to Launch Services -- which is outselling Space Systems 2-to-1!

    So what does that mean for Rocket Lab? Not only will revenue growth accelerate, but the profits Rocket Lab earns on that revenue will accelerate even more (thanks to a higher profit margin).

    In a recent development, and the good news doesn't end there. Rocket Lab generated positive operating cash flow in Q3 2026 -- $7.2 million. It's not a big number. It's not positive free cash flow. But this is the first time Rocket Lab has generated positive operating cash flow for a full quarter. Once it grows beyond capital investment costs, Rocket Lab will finally become FCF-positive.

    I have publicly predicted that Rocket Lab will turn generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) profitable and FCF positive in 2027 after it completes its acquisition of Iridium Communications and adds Iridium's revenue and profit streams to its own.

    Recent findings suggest that in the meantime, Rocket Lab's Q4 guidance will show steady progress toward its goal. Turning to guidance, management predicts quarterly revenue between $270 million and $290 million, with gross margins from Launch Services and Space Systems blending to average 34%-36%.

    According to recent reports, this implies gross profit of about $98 million for the quarter. If operating costs reach $168 million -- as management also predicts -- this will prevent Rocket Lab from turning profitable in Q4. I'd similarly expect operating cash flow to be eclipsed by capital spending costs, which are averaging more than $30 million per quarter right now -- so you can expect no FCF in Q4, either.

    NASDAQ · As of 10:00 AM ET 11/20/26.

    Recent findings suggest that all that stated, Rocket Lab is on the right trajectory for profit. Sales are rising, profit margins are rising too, and Rocket Lab has demonstrated that it can generate positive operating cash flow. All it needs now is to scale that up past capital requirements. Once Iridium Communications is brought in-house, I expect that mission to be accomplished.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Alex Carchidi – Nov 20, 2026 at 7:30AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Hyperliquid ›.

    In a recent development, when speaking on a podcast earlier this month, Matt Hougan, chief investment officer of crypto asset manager Bitwise, stated that he thinks Hyperliquid (HYPE -7.96%) could become the next Amazon (AMZN -0.12%) thanks to its habit of expanding beyond crypto perpetual futures into real-world assets and prediction markets. That stance meshes cleanly with the view of Hyperliquid Labs' co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Jeff Yan, who wants it to become the "house all of finance." His preferred method for accomplishing that goal closely mirrors Amazon's marketplace model, in which sellers use the firm's infrastructure to connect with their target buyers, facilitating transactions from which the platform takes a cut of the proceeds.

    Recent findings suggest that hougan is probably correct about Hyperliquid's potential. Here's why, and how realizing that potential is likely to play out.

    Sources indicate that hyperliquid is a decentralized exchange that specializes in perpetual futures contracts, or perps, which are a type of financial derivative. People pay fees to trade them, and nearly all of the resulting revenue is used to buy back HYPE coins on the open market, like a stock buyback. The exchange earned $72.6 million in revenue during the 30-day period ended Nov. 19, and its coin is up by about 75% during the past 12 months.

    Third-party merchants do much of Amazon's selling. Hyperliquid's equivalent is letting other companies commit the capital that's needed to create new markets on its platform, using its infrastructure. For now, new perpetuals markets and prediction markets are supported on Hyperliquid, and to launch one, a developer must stake 500,000 HYPE, worth about $34.4 million as of Nov. 19, which must stay locked for at least 183 days and can be rejected by validators if the market developer misbehaves. Then, those third parties are entitled to a portion of the fees generated by trading on the markets they funded.

    CRYPTO · As of 9:57 AM ET 11/20/26.

    Sources indicate that hyperliquid also offers a marketplace of "vaults." Vaults let anyone with $100 open an investment fund that others can invest in, almost like a mini hedge fund. The fund's manager is entitled to their portion of the fund's profits, and investors can easily screen hundreds of vaults to find those with the performance record and asset mix they prefer.

    So in many ways, Hyperliquid is already following Amazon's business plan within its own domain.

    According to recent reports, as of October, more than 261 decentralized crypto exchanges offering perpetual futures trading have introduced since Hyperliquid opened in 2022. But it still holds a 57% share of open interest in perps (the value of contracts outstanding) across decentralized perpetual futures exchanges.

    This is to say that Hyperliquid's competitors are myriad and growing in number, and have always been so, and likely always will be. Plus, there are many powerful competitors aiming to achieve much the same outcome as Hyperliquid using other approaches. That means its margins may always be under pressure, and its growth may always be contested by competitors.

    According to recent reports, but the same was also true for Amazon in its early days, and that didn't stop it. So while it's probably not for the best to bet the farm on Hyperliquid becoming the Amazon of decentralized finance, it's certainly on track to accomplish just that.

    #4230. AI For Math Proofs: Organized Monkeys Or Superhuman Genius?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (997 w)

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    AI For Math Proofs: Organized Monkeys Or Superhuman Genius?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (997 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ambuj Kumar, Simbian.ai co-founder and CEO, pioneered confidential computing, and builds AI agents to counter AI threats.
    • On October 6, 2026, OpenAI posted over 700 AI-written math manuscripts.
    • According to recent reports, this doesn’t mean that mathematicians are celebrating.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ambuj Kumar, Simbian.ai co-founder and CEO, pioneered confidential computing, and builds AI agents to counter AI threats.

    On October 6, 2026, OpenAI posted over 700 AI-written math manuscripts. About 300 come with proofs in Lean, a language a computer can check line by line. One claims a zero-free region for the Riemann zeta function, where the real part exceeds 7/8, a partial result related to the long-standing Riemann hypothesis. Months earlier, an unreleased Claude model raised the proven share of zeta zeros on the critical line from 41.6% to 67.2%, with a Lean proof.

    According to recent reports, this doesn’t mean that mathematicians are celebrating. In September, Terence Tao and 24 other Fields Medalists signed a declaration saying that “the goals of the AI companies and the goals of the mathematical community are severely misaligned.” In a lecture at Caltech on October 9, Tao went further: “Further blind optimization of problem-solving alone is now actively harmful to the long-term health of mathematics.”.

    According to recent reports, so, are these machines geniuses? To judge that, start with how an LLM learns math.​.

    ​Many labs train reasoning models using reinforcement learning, rewarding models when they produce correct answers. The approach works particularly well when those answers can be objectively verified. Whether an essay is good or a security alert is real is a judgment call, and a noisy reward teaches a noisy model.

    Math offers a particularly useful advantage: When a proof is formalized in Lean, its checker can determine whether the argument follows from the stated assumptions, without requiring a human to review every step. ​It should therefore be no surprise that models trained this way can now produce solutions to problems that have stumped generations of mathematicians.​.

    In a recent development, however, it also creates a problem. When proofs are checked automatically, the model only has to be right once, and you can keep it trying for as long as you can pay for those GPUs. Give enough monkeys enough typewriters, and one will eventually type Hamlet. In practice it never happens, because probability is so low we would have to wait for trillions of years.

    Recent findings suggest that LLMs are stochastic systems that can generate mathematical arguments and Lean proof attempts. Many attempts will fail, but a model that can produce sufficiently promising candidates can be paired with an automated checker to identify formally valid results.​ How many attempts would it take to solve a famous problem? What if a lab can spend tens of millions of dollars on compute, while successful announcements strengthen perceptions of its AI capabilities and potentially improve its competitive position? Those economics justify a very large search.

    According to recent reports, only the successful results receive individual attention. The thousand failed tries, the tokens burned and the size of the model running the search largely stay out of view.​​.

    Sources indicate that ​None of this is an accusation. Math has long been the clearest test of intelligence, and labs should test their models on it.

    Industry observers note that the trouble is what we use math to measure. We admire mathematicians like Terence Tao for their ability to develop insights and solve problems that might take others months or years to understand. When Ramanujan filled notebooks with identities that took others decades to prove, part of the wonder was how little he seemed to need.​.

    In a recent development, the labs only disclose some of the cost, but not enough. Anthropic indicates its zeta result took 31 million output tokens, after a first session tried 650 ideas without success. OpenAI says its model averaged three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking per result. Neither lab has mentioned how major its model is. OpenAI has not published its prompts or per-result compute, although an advisory group of mathematicians at the Institute for Advanced Study asked for both on September 29.​.

    It has been revealed that A mathematician who proves a theorem after a month of drafts has run a 20-watt brain for that month. A hypothetical 10-trillion-parameter model that needs a hundred attempts could consume vastly more energy, depending on the hardware and compute involved. From outside, the two announcements look the same, and nothing tells us whether we are looking at a mind like Ramanujan’s or a well-organized room of monkeys.​.

    ​I propose that every AI-generated proof ship with a disclosure card, like a security researcher publishes an advisory for every vulnerability they disclose.​.

    According to recent reports, the security world has developed a useful model for this. CVE provides standardized identifiers for publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, while CVSS offers a common framework for assessing their severity. Coordinated disclosure processes also establish expectations for documenting findings, notifying affected parties and appropriately attributing researchers.​.

    In a recent development, A similar discipline can be followed here. arXiv could add a metadata field for AI-assisted proofs, journals like the Annals of Mathematics could require a card at submission and the Lean mathlib community could require disclosure in every pull request that credits an AI contributor.

    It has been revealed that defining what counts as an attempt will be hard, though, and labs will not shy away from calling model size and per-result compute trade secrets. Also, the lab that discloses first will look worse than the one that stays silent, which is why the first standard has to come from a venue that can refuse to publish without the card.

    Once cost sits next to every result, a small model’s first-try proof outranks a giant model’s hundredth try, and labs have a reason to build small models that find short proofs mathematicians can read and build on. Until a result comes with its card, and until these models work alongside mathematicians, I believe we should hold back the respect we reserve for people who solve problems the traditional way.​​​.

    It has been revealed that forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

    Should Bitcoin (BTC -3.69%), recommended by Team Hidden Gems, come up between the turkey and the pie next week, expect at least one relative to mention the recent slide—probably with some satisfaction. The price fell as low as $62,000 late Saturday, capping a sixth straight week of declines, and dipped below that level Thursday night.

    It has been revealed that step back a little, and the picture gets harder to look at. Bitcoin hit a record of about $126,000 on Oct. 6, 2025, and it’s now worth less than half that, down more than a quarter for the year. Since 2016, only November 2022, the month the FTX exchange collapsed, got off to a worse start.What knocked Bitcoin down?

    There wasn't a single shock behind this so much as a pile-up, and most of the pressure started outside the crypto world entirely.

    Recent findings suggest that the first domino was tech, with the decline beginning in late October, when worries about AI valuations and spending pulled tech stocks lower, and leadership turmoil at Nvidia (NVDA -3.43%) only made investors more nervous about risk. On top of that, hotter-than-expected inflation pushed the dollar index to its highest level since April 2025. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem also said several rate hikes may be needed before next spring.

    Industry observers note that crypto had a scare of its own when the $6.3 billion Binance hack in late October—the largest crypto heist on record—led investors to convert stablecoins back into traditional currency, according to Grayscale. Spot Bitcoin ETFs saw about $1.91 billion in net outflows over seven straight trading days through Nov. 13.

    What turned a slide into a rout, though, was borrowed money. Once Bitcoin broke below its 200-day moving average near $73,000, forced selling of leveraged positions took over.Wall Street hasn’t walked away.

    According to recent reports, in October, J.P. Morgan Asset Management, part of JPMorgan Chase (JPM -0.48%) and hardly a crypto fund, issued its first-ever 10-year return forecast for Bitcoin, calling for 10% a year, compounded, compared with 5.5% for gold. Strategists Sheena Shah and Dennis Cristallo wrote that "bitcoin is the anchor of the crypto ecosystem.".

    Recent findings suggest that it isn't a moonshot call, either, and JPMorgan was upfront about the caveats, pegging Bitcoin's volatility at 55% and noting that its unstable correlations still keep it out of most portfolios. Still, the asset-management arm of the largest U.S. bank now considers Bitcoin worth modeling a full decade out.

    Consider what a few major financial firms actually did over the past several months.

    Industry observers note that charles Schwab (SCHW +0.14%) finished rolling out spot Bitcoin and Ethereum(ETH -4.23%) trading to its retail clients in October. "All clients can now access Schwab Crypto," CEO Rick Wurster mentioned on Oct. 15, and the company is adding crypto transfers and three more coins by year-end. Its executives estimate that Schwab clients already hold about 20% of all U.S. spot crypto ETP assets, which gives a sense of how much demand was there to begin with.

    Deutsche Bank (DB -0.73%) switched on Bitcoin and Ethereum custody for paying institutional clients on Nov. 11, right in the middle of the selloff. Paul Maley, its global head of trust and securities services, stated the bank aims to build "a fully integrated, regulated ecosystem" for digital assets, and it prepares to bring the service to Asia. Over at Morgan Stanley(MS -2.26%), the E*Trade platform rolled out crypto trading in July through crypto infrastructure firm Zerohash.What the biggest holder is doing.

    Recent findings suggest that strategy(MSTR -1.37%), the largest corporate owner of Bitcoin, is still buying, though at a much slower clip than it used to. It bought 485 BTC for $33.4 million between Nov. 9 and Nov. 15, at an average of $68,887 per coin, according to a regulatory filing on Monday, after picking up 1,036 BTC the week before. The treasury company now holds 850,849 BTC, about 4% of the 21 million that will ever exist.

    Sources indicate that so Strategy hasn’t capitulated, but it isn’t a backstop anyone should count on. Its average cost is $75,452 per coin, leaving its position roughly 15% underwater at about $64,000. Its buying also depends on raising money from investors, which gets harder when its own stock is down.

    It has been revealed that if you own some Bitcoin, your time horizon should be among your biggest considerations. Drops of 50% or more have been part of owning Bitcoin since its earliest days, so if you bought it to hold for five or 10 years, this drawdown is part of the deal you signed up for. Position size matters just as much, because the right amount is one you could hold through another leg down without needing to sell.

    Sources indicate that finally, Fools know to steer clear of leverage with any speculative instrument. This month's worst damage landed on traders using borrowed money, while investors who owned their coins outright got a scary-looking statement rather than a margin call.

    In a recent development, motley Fool co-founder and CEO Tom Gardner made a similar point during his Quarterly Call last December, when this drawdown was still in its early weeks. He traced Bitcoin’s wild swings to the same kind of borrowed money that did the damage this month: when the price runs, “people start to lever up and think, this is the time when I’ll triple my money in four months. That margin gets exposed, and the asset is very volatile.” He drew a distinction worth holding onto: “Bitcoin is not a stable store of value. But I do believe it is a long-term store of value.”.

    Sources indicate that the average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.24% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points lower than yesterday and three basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.).

    A significant drop is eye-catching, but you should consider mortgage interest rates' overall direction, not just what's going on today. While the economy never sleeps, markets are closed on the weekends. The rates you see Friday are unlikely to change much (if at all) until Monday.

For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

    It has been revealed that next week, the Nerds are waiting for the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, due out Wednesday. It's the Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation, so investors will be watching closely. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but lenders anticipate its decisions, so mortgage rates often move before the Fed acts. Stubbornly high inflation is a major reason why we’re seeing upward pressure on mortgage rates right now.

    It has been revealed that if PCE shows inflation comes in hotter than expected, mortgage rates could climb as markets anticipate further Fed rate hikes. (An increase to the federal funds rate is already widely expected at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting.) A cooler reading could ease some pressure on mortgage rates for now.

    Recent findings suggest that I’m not getting my hopes up too high for meaningfully lower inflation, though. Last week's Producer Price Index showed wholesale inflation climbed 6.5% over the past year — its fastest pace in four years. Wholesale inflation measures the price businesses pay for things. When businesses’ costs go up, they could pass those along to consumers in the form of higher prices — keeping the flames of inflation alive.

    Whether Wednesday's PCE brings relief or another helping of bad inflation news, we'll know before the turkey hits the table on Thursday.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Stefon Walters – Nov 20, 2026 at 7:40AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Altria Group ›.

    Recent findings suggest that altria (MO +0.72%) is one of the market's marquee dividend stocks. In fact, many investors would tell you that Altria's dividend is the only reason to invest, even though the stock price surged more than 33% this year (as of Nov. 18). If Altria continues its impressive run, it'll be its best-performing year since its 2008 Philip Morris International (PM +0.59%) spinoff.

    Altria's stock price run won't be the norm, but its dividend is as consistent as it gets, with the company being a Dividend King (a company with at least 50 consecutive years of dividend increases). It routinely offers one of the higher yields among S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.06%) companies and could be a good income play for patient investors. Here's how much it could pay out in dividends over the next decade with a $10,000 investment.

    At Altria's price at the time of writing, $10,000 would buy about 130 shares, so we'll use that for our example. At Altria's annualized payout of $4.44 ($1.11 quarterly), those shares would pay $577.20. If we assume Altria increases its annual dividend by 5% each year (it has averaged more than 6% annually over the past decade), here's how much you could expect in annual cash payouts:.

    With a single $10,000 investment, you would've received close to $7,260 in cash payouts over a decade. The real magic, though, happens when you reinvest your dividends back into the stock, giving them a chance to earn dividends on them. In this scenario, had you reinvested dividends from year 1, your final investment value would easily be thousands more than $17,260 (original $10,000 investment plus $7,260 in cash payouts).

    Recent findings suggest that altria is uniquely positioned as the country's largest tobacco producer, leading an industry at a crossroads. On one end, you have declining smoking rates in U.S. adults. According to the CDC, 42.4% of U.S. adults smoked in 1965. Now, that has dropped to 9.9%.

    When you're the country's largest cigarette producer, that decline has a noticeable impact on business.

    Industry observers note that on the other end, tobacco people are very loyal and like what they like. Someone who smokes Marlboro Red or Black & Mild cigars (two of Altria's most popular brands) will typically buy them, even if prices go up. Of course, consumers have financial limits, but for the most part, this dynamic has given Altria the pricing power to offset some of its volume decline.

    Altria hasn't done a great job establishing a smoke-free alternative to compete with popular brands like Philip Morris International's Zyn, but it isn't time to ring the alarm yet. Altria has enough time and more than enough resources to make something happen.

    If you're looking for a good income investment, Altria is a buy. It knows its appeal is its dividend, so it's as shareholder-friendly as they come. I don't expect that to change in the foreseeable future.
