    • Industry observers note that robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

    According to recent reports, here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

    Industry observers note that robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

    Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

    In a recent development, robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

    Recent findings suggest that transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

    Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

    Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

    According to recent reports, net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

    —With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney.

    #4224. Industry News: Moving Toward Autonomous Planning Without Losing Sight Of ROI

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1061 w)

    EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Moving Toward Autonomous Planning Without Losing Sight Of ROI

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1061 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that alex Koshulko, Ph.D, is a supply chain planning expert with 10+ years of experience.
    • What if your AI agents hit their KPIs and still cost your company $330,000?
    • In a recent development, in a simulation published by Supply Chain Management Review, five AI agents represented different supply chain functions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that alex Koshulko, Ph.D, is a supply chain planning expert with 10+ years of experience. CEO and co-founder of Streamline.

    What if your AI agents hit their KPIs and still cost your company $330,000?

    In a recent development, in a simulation published by Supply Chain Management Review, five AI agents represented different supply chain functions. Four improved their performance metrics, yet the simulated company’s EBITDA fell by approximately $330,000 compared with a scenario where their objectives were aligned. Each function pursued its own targets at the expense of the overall business.

    Industry observers note that for me, this exposes one of the challenges in autonomous planning. An agent can perform its assigned task successfully while making decisions that hurt the company’s financial performance.

    As businesses give AI more authority, they need to understand what those decisions will cost, what they will improve and how to measure the results.

    Ask a planner why they cut last week’s purchase order by 20%, and you may hear reasons that the planning system doesn’t fully capture. An AI agent reviewing the same order needs the numbers and the context behind them.

    Companies preparing for autonomous planning have good reason to start with data management. McKinsey found that approximately 65% of advanced planning system programs failed to achieve their expected ROI, with poor data management among the five leading causes.

    Fixing the data addresses part of the challenge. But how do you give an agent the knowledge planners use to interpret it and assess the consequences of their decisions?

    Industry observers note that the solution might be a contextual layer that brings together ERP data, input from planners and simulation results that show how different planning choices could affect operations and finances. Building it requires mature processes, but the work can improve them.

    Sources indicate that the goal is to give agents enough context to evaluate the financial consequences of their actions before execution, with people responsible for setting objectives and constraints. But even then, forecasts and simulations cannot guarantee the outcome. Business results must determine when agents receive greater authority.

    In a recent development, A planner may spend time exporting reports, reconciling figures and obtaining approvals because the systems involved cannot share information directly. An AI agent with access to the relevant data and business context can handle parts of that work without following the same sequence of steps.

    Before delegating a workflow, ask: if an agent had direct access to the right information, would we design the process the same way?

    Gartner predicts that cross-functional multiagent systems will execute 35% of enterprise workflows with minimal human approvals by 2030, up from 3% in 2025. As companies delegate more work to agents, they need to distinguish manual steps imposed by system limitations from controls that protect business outcomes.

    Data transfers and duplicate checks may no longer require human effort, but approvals tied to financial exposure, customer commitments or difficult-to-reverse decisions serve a purpose. These distinctions should shape the workflow before an agent takes over its execution.

    Recent findings suggest that I suggest beginning with a narrow pilot where the consequences of a wrong decision are manageable and can be detected rapidly. Replenishing a stable product is a more practical starting point than allocating scarce inventory among strategic customers during a disruption.

    It has been revealed that the pilot should show whether the business outcome improved against a baseline. Before expanding its authority, the tech giant should test how the agent responds when demand, supply conditions or business constraints change.

    Industry observers note that the level of autonomy needs to reflect the risks of each decision. A firm might allow an agent to handle replenishment within defined limits, require planner approval for higher-value orders and keep strategic allocation decisions under human control.

    Recent findings suggest that gartner’s forecast illustrates how limited autonomous decision-making is expected to remain. While 83% of surveyed organizations had already invested at least $3 million in planning automation, including AI, Gartner expects only 5% of organizations implementing supply chain planning automation to allow systems to make at least 10% of planning decisions autonomously by 2030.

    When financial performance improves after an AI rollout, how much of that improvement can we credit to the agent? Inventory may have fallen because demand weakened or supplier terms changed. Both factors need to be accounted for when calculating the agent’s contribution.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s also worth looking at the impact on working capital and operating costs. Lower inventory can free up cash, but if it leads to emergency shipments or missed orders, those consequences belong in the assessment, too. So do the costs of deploying and operating AI.

    Sources indicate that A purchasing decision may take weeks to reveal whether it protected service levels or created excess stock. During that time, an agent could make dozens of similar decisions before the business sees the consequences. Evaluate ROI across the relevant purchasing and replenishment cycles, allowing enough time to measure the financial outcomes of those decisions, including the cost of correcting errors.

    Recent findings suggest that gartner predicts that by 2029, 60% of supply chain planner roles will shift from operational execution to strategic oversight as autonomous planning systems take over routine decisions.​ As a result, I expect planners to spend more time setting the boundaries for autonomous execution. They will define spending limits, decide when human intervention is necessary and review results across planning cycles.​.

    Sources indicate that A planner who once approved individual purchase orders may soon oversee hundreds of decisions made by AI agents. In our practice, for example, a North American CPG manufacturer increased the number of forecast edits by more than 100 times through the use of AI agents. This illustrates how agents can expand the scale of planning activity, but it also makes oversight more important. Planners will need to recognize when established rules require adjustment, whether because supplier conditions have shifted, customer priorities have changed or financial results no longer justify the current approach.​.

    Industry observers note that AI agents will not eliminate the need for human judgment in supply chain planning. While they have tremendous potential in the supply chain, ​their value will depend on how effectively organizations combine autonomous execution with human oversight.​​​​.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 10 stocks we like better than Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF ›.
    • Industry observers note that investing in the stock market is interesting because not all participants share the same objectives.
    • Maybe you sit right in the middle of the spectrum: Your goal is to have growth and income exposure.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Neil Patel – Nov 20, 2026 at 7:45AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF ›.

    Industry observers note that investing in the stock market is interesting because not all participants share the same objectives. Some are fully focused on achieving the highest returns, which will push them to take on more risk. There are other investors, however, who want to own assets that generate steady income. This will lead them to discover stable dividend-paying stocks.

    Maybe you sit right in the middle of the spectrum: Your goal is to have growth and income exposure. But you don't want to spend time picking individual stocks. Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) might be the answer. Here's what I believe is the simplest ETF portfolio to build for growth and income.

    According to recent reports, to find a solid growth ETF, you don't have to look very far. The Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF (VUG -0.53%) is a good choice. It charges an expense ratio of 0.03%. I suggest using half of your available cash to buy shares in this investment vehicle.

    Recent findings suggest that this ETF tracks the performance of the Morningstar (MORN +1.99%) U.S. Large Cap Growth Index. It contains 135 different stocks in businesses that have increased revenue and profits at above-average rates in the past.

    The performance is notable: In the last decade, the Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF has generated a total return of 399% (as of Nov. 16). The S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.06%) had a total return of 308% by comparison. No one knows if the superior performance will continue, but you ignore historical trends at your own peril.

    The technology sector represents 69% of this Vanguard ETF, with consumer discretionary (13% weighting) a distant second. This shouldn't exactly come as a surprise. Many of the top growth stocks operate in tech-related industries.

    The risk is that markets are changing rapidly, challenging established competitive advantages. On the other hand, the advantage is that there is significant potential in the long run.

    Recent findings suggest that by owning this ETF, investors will instantly build exposure to the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. Apple (AAPL +0.30%), Nvidia (NVDA -2.66%), and Microsoft (MSFT +0.77%), which combine for 37% of the Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF, are the three largest positions. While the degrees vary, they are all positioned to benefit from the secular AI trend, an area of the market that is hard to avoid if you're craving growth.

    NYSEMKT · As of 9:58 AM ET 11/20/26.

    For the income part of the equation, consider the Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (SCHD +1.26%)for the other half of your cash position. This ETF, which carries an expense ratio of 0.06%, is an attractive option for those seeking income.

    Recent findings suggest that the Schwab ETF follows the Dow Jones U.S. Dividend 100 Index. Companies are screened based on different fundamental factors, a sign of their financial strength that can be valuable in times of economic stress. And they're required to have paid dividends in 10 straight years.

    In a recent development, over the last decade, the ETF's total return came in at 257%. While you give up some opportunity on the capital appreciation front, you capture a healthy 2.95% trailing-12-month dividend yield. That's almost three times more income than the S&P 500 index will get you. The ETF's payout has also doubled in the last decade.

    If you want to explore options outside the public equity market that are more stable, consider a fixed-income ETF. The iShares Trust-iShares 0-3 Month Treasury Bond ETF (SGOV +0.03%), charging an expense ratio of 0.09%, is compelling. It owns short-term Treasury bills. The trailing-one-year dividend yield of 3.63% is much higher than what you'll receive from the Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF. However, there is no growth potential here.

    Whether you choose one or both of the Schwab and iShares ETFs for income, pairing your choice with the Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF creates a well-rounded portfolio. Two objectives will be satisfied simultaneously.

    Nvidia and Micron Can't Make AI Chips Without This Growth Stock. Here's Why It Could Soar.

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that nvidia (NVDA -3.43%) and Micron Technology (MU -6.35%) both make chips that are essential to the continued AI build-out, but their chips couldn't be more different.
    • Recent findings suggest that while Micron prints its chips itself, Nvidia contracts chip manufacturing to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing.
    • The company is growing quickly, but the market may still underappreciate the opportunity ahead for the business, and the stock could soar from here.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Adam Levy – Nov 20, 2026 at 8:00AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Applied Materials ›.

    Recent findings suggest that nvidia (NVDA -3.43%) and Micron Technology (MU -6.35%) both make chips that are essential to the continued AI build-out, but their chips couldn't be more different. Nvidia makes advanced logic chips and graphics processing units (GPUs) used for training and inference of large language models. Micron makes memory chips, and demand for its high-bandwidth chips has soared, as the ability to quickly access large volumes of data for training and inference has become a bottleneck in the continued development of AI.

    Recent findings suggest that while Micron prints its chips itself, Nvidia contracts chip manufacturing to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing. However, there's one organization neither could produce its chips without: Applied Materials (AMAT -4.70%). The company supplies manufacturers such as Micron and Nvidia's partner, TSMC, with a wide range of wafer fabrication equipment.

    The company is growing quickly, but the market may still underappreciate the opportunity ahead for the business, and the stock could soar from here.

    Applied Materials holds a broad portfolio of wafer fabrication equipment that's used by both logic chipmakers like Nvidia and memory chipmakers like Micron. As Micron and other memory chipmakers respond to the spike in demand for their chips, Applied's share of semiconductor system sales for DRAM and flash memory chipmaking equipment climbed to 42% of sales in the company's fiscal fourth quarter. That's despite heavy spending from advanced logic chipmakers like TSMC as well.

    Recent findings suggest that overall, Applied Materials' revenue climbed 21% in 2026, but that growth has accelerated sharply every quarter. Revenue was up 53% year over year in Q4. What's more, management expects 2027 to come in strong as well. Its first-quarter outlook calls for $11.1 billion in revenue at the midpoint, up 22% from last year. But it expects the market for wafer fabrication equipment to grow 30% overall for the full year and to gain market share, implying revenue acceleration throughout the year.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:55 AM ET 11/20/26.

    Industry observers note that applied's broad portfolio of equipment positions it well to gain market share in the fast-growing industry. It's the only equipment maker that competes across all three market segments: etch, deposition, and process control. Its size gives it the advantage of investing more in research and development than its competitors, while working closely with manufacturers to build integrated solutions that save floor space. Those solutions increase switching costs for manufacturers, locking them into Applied's products and servicing.

    In the longer run, management expects its gross margin to expand by five percentage points from 2025 to 2030, while operating margin expands by 10 percentage points during the same period. Combined with the robust outlook for revenue growth driven by expected spending on artificial intelligence, Applied should deliver very strong net income growth and free cash flow. Management is committed to returning excess free cash flow to shareholders over time, reducing its share count, and further boosting earnings per share.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:55 AM ET 11/20/26.

    Sources indicate that applied Materials stock currently trades for less than 20 times forward earnings estimates. That's despite expectations that earnings per share will grow more than 46% over the next year and another 28% the following year.

    That low multiple is due to the cyclical nature of the business, and there's a significant risk that its equipment sales growth will taper as AI spending stabilizes and capacity constraints ease. That noted, the firm's services revenue acts as a ballast, providing a consistent stream of revenue, as its equipment must be serviced regularly to maintain precision.

    Recent findings suggest that that said, an earnings multiple of 20 is closer to its mid-cycle multiple, and the outlook for wafer fabrication equipment spending (as well as analysts' outlooks) indicates we're closer to the start of an up cycle in earnings. Importantly, the stock price could fall to about 12 times trailing earnings by the end of fiscal 2029 and still trade at roughly the same price as today. If it trades closer to the mid-cycle multiple of 20, that's upside of 63% from here. In my opinion, that's somewhat conservative considering the outlook for equipment demand.

    #4213. Your AI Isn’t Misbehaving; It’s Obeying

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1029 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    Your AI Isn’t Misbehaving; It’s Obeying

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that global Field CISO at Mimecast.
    • In a recent development, ​Imagine an employee creates an AI agent to accelerate customer renewals.
    • Then it exposes one customer’s information while working on another.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that global Field CISO at Mimecast. Creator of Risk Reframing. 20+ years across intelligence agencies, cybersecurity, and executive leadership.

    In a recent development, ​Imagine an employee creates an AI agent to accelerate customer renewals. It reads account histories, reviews support cases, drafts recommendations and updates the CRM. It performs consistently, uses only approved tools and has valid credentials.

    Then it exposes one customer’s information while working on another. The security team investigates. There is no compromised identity, no anomalous login, no unauthorized connection.

    According to recent reports, in August, NIST published its “Human-Centered Cybersecurity Guidelines and Resources Concept Paper,” which argued that decades of security programs have treated people as vulnerabilities to be trained and tested, and the breaches keep coming anyway. Awareness training sets “unrealistic expectations that employees will always make the ‘right’ decisions,” while the real root causes (unusable processes, disruptive controls, a culture nobody absorbed) go unaddressed.

    It’s a paper about end users, but read next to AI agents; it describes the same failure one layer removed. The reflex to scrutinize the person closest to the failure—the employee who clicked, the agent that acted—lets the design decision upstream of them off the hook. For agentic AI, that decision is provisioning: the first decision, made before any systems act, when a person defines what an agent is for, what it can touch and where its authority ends. Call the practice of getting it right provisioning assurance.

    In a recent development, most security programs observe activity: what an identity accessed, whether behavior violated policy. AI agents complicate that because they don’t just exercise access; they interpret objectives and act on someone’s behalf, executing the judgment they were given more faithfully than any human would.

    Before an agent acts, a person has already decided its purpose, permissions and operating conditions (explicitly, or casually in a prompt or an approval screen). The agent inherits them either way. Provisioning is not only technical setup; it’s the moment human judgment becomes machine authority. Selecting “allow” takes a second. The authority it creates operates repeatedly, at scale.

    Recent findings suggest that in September, I argued every AI incident runs on two timelines: the one we investigate and the one that set it in motion. Here’s the version of that split that matters for provisioning: There’s the timeline we know how to read (alerts, logs, containment) and an earlier one, often six months back or longer, when someone decided what the agent was for, what access it would hold and what failure was tolerable. Monitoring tells us what happened after that authority was granted. It doesn’t tell us whether granting it was sound.

    In a recent development, an agent doesn’t need to misbehave to cause harm. One instructed to speed up support-case resolution may prioritize speed exactly as directed while overlooking contractual restrictions or a customer’s downstream needs. It may even look successful by the metric it was given.

    It has been revealed that the renewals agents show where the failure lives: in the original judgment—an objective too narrow, boundaries incomplete, trade-offs never made explicit, no one accountable for the outcome. None of that produces an anomaly. The agent scores clean because it’s faithfully executing a defective charter, and most AI governance programs are built to catch an agent drifting from its instructions, not one whose instructions are the source of the risk.

    Seeing that judgment means comparing three versions of an agent’s authority: declared authority (what the provisioner states it does), inferred authority (what its permissions and connections actually make possible) and observed authority (what it does in practice). An agent is described as a feedback summarizer (declared). It can read and modify CRM records and message a collaboration platform (inferred). It starts exporting customer records to an outside environment (observed).

    That distinction clarifies who owns the fix. Behavioral drift (an agent departing its baseline or instructions) deserves monitoring and containment. Judgment drift (an employee changes roles, a project ends, an approval step gets removed but the agent’s authority stays put) calls for renewed authorization, not containment. Provisioning failure—original purpose or boundaries were inadequate—requires revisiting the human decision itself. Treat all three as agent-behavior problems, and you fix the symptom, not the judgment.

    It has been revealed that every material expansion of authority (a newly introduced connector, read access becoming write access, an approval checkpoint removed, ownership transferred) is a new provisioning event, whether or not the organization recognizes it. This matters most when people move: An agent built for a legitimate purpose can keep running on valid credentials long after its creator changes roles or leaves, its authority sitting there un-renewed and unclaimed. The question isn’t just “Is the agent still running?” It’s “Who is renewing the judgment that allows it to run?” Renewal isn’t remediation: It’s what you do because time passed.

    Recent findings suggest that inventories are the right start: You can’t govern what you can’t see. Provisioning assurance is the next step: preserving the decision behind the agent, not just the agent itself. For every agent with meaningful authority, leaders should be able to answer four questions. Who owns its authority and consequences? What outcome was it authorized to pursue? What’s explicitly outside its scope? And what event triggers reauthorization or retirement? Most of this can be inferred from identity and configuration. The human’s job is to confirm what technology can’t: purpose, boundaries, accountability.

    Industry observers note that that’s provisioning assurance: evaluating whether machine authority rests on identifiable ownership, an adequate purpose and a defined moment for renewal. The goal isn’t to score the employee. It’s to assess the quality of the decision.

    NIST is right that stronger cybersecurity starts with people. An agent’s behavior tells us what happened. Its provisioning tells us what human judgment became capable of doing. Assurance tells us whether that judgment was sound. The next generation of AI governance can’t begin with the agent’s first action—by then, the most consequential decision has already been made. Organizations don’t just inherit technology. They inherit authored judgment. Increasingly, that judgment can act.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Jack Delaney – Nov 20, 2026 at 8:13AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

    According to recent reports, on Thursday, Nov. 19, Anthropic (ANT -5.45%) opened to the public at $111.50 per share. The stock price touched $115.10 at one point during the day, then fell below $100, closing at $97.17.

    Industry observers note that while major news outlets report Anthropic shares climbed 17% on the day, for any retail investor who bought $1,000 worth of stock, there's a good chance they've already lost money. This is why that disconnect exists, and what to consider after Anthropic's first day as a publicly traded company.

    The returns for retail investors may differ from those reported by major news outlets due to the gap between the initial public offering (IPO) price and the price at which Anthropic shares opened to the public.

    The IPO pricing was set at $83, a level typically reserved for high-net-worth individuals and large institutions. For that group, with Anthropic closing at $97.17 per share, their return was 17%.

    Let's say a retail investor bought $1,000 worth of stock, and their entire order was filled at the opening price of $111.50. That would give them approximately nine shares. At a closing price of $97.17, that $1,000 investment would have declined to around $870.

    Fortunately, for investors who plan to hold for the long haul, day one won't make or break an investment.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:55 AM ET 11/20/26.

    Meta Platforms (META -1.81%) is one of the best examples of having a rough IPO and a tough few months of trading before ultimately rewarding long-term investors.

    Sources indicate that when it went public as Facebook in May 2012, it was chaotic. On the very first day of trading, a glitch delayed the public offering by 30 minutes, and some traders didn't receive confirmation that their trades had gone through. The stock price finished flat on the day, and things only got worse from there. According to research from The Motley Fool, out of the 10 largest IPOs by capital raised to date, Meta has had the worst three-month post-IPO performance, with shares down 47%.

    Recent findings suggest that that stated, the good news for anyone who still had conviction in the company was that they were handsomely rewarded. Five years after its public debut, the stock price was up 289%. Then, by May 2026, about 14 years after the IPO, the stock price had climbed 1,572%.

    According to recent reports, what that tells investors about Anthropic is that it's not the first day of trading, or even the first few months, that will determine whether the company was a good investment. It will take years to find out, making it the best fit for an investor who can handle price swings and has a patient approach.

    #4206. Coming Out of Retirement in 2027? 3 Things to Brace Yourself For.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (687 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fool ↗ Open Full Page

    Coming Out of Retirement in 2027? 3 Things to Brace Yourself For.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By Kailey Hagen, CFP® – Nov 20, 2026 at 8:15AM EST.
    • In a recent development, coming out of retirement might not have been part of the plan for you, but it’s one of your best options if you find yourself draining your savings faster than you anticipated.
    • In a recent development, but there can be a few drawbacks to coming out of retirement that are worth being aware of before you rejoin the workforce.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Kailey Hagen, CFP® – Nov 20, 2026 at 8:15AM EST.

    In a recent development, coming out of retirement might not have been part of the plan for you, but it’s one of your best options if you find yourself draining your savings faster than you anticipated. A steady paycheck can slow the drain on your retirement accounts, and some people find they enjoy the sense of purpose and opportunity to socialize that a job can bring.

    In a recent development, but there can be a few drawbacks to coming out of retirement that are worth being aware of before you rejoin the workforce. The following three things are unlikely to be deal-breakers, but they may force you to rethink your budget going forward.

    If you've been out of the workforce for years or even decades, finding upcoming employment could take some time. This is especially true if you work in an industry where things change rapidly. You may have to live off your savings for longer than you planned while trying to find new employment.

    You can increase your odds of success by staying up to date with the latest industry trends and, if possible, pursuing advanced certifications. Or, if you don't need a ton of extra income, look outside your industry for new opportunities you may not have considered before. Part-time or remote work could give you some flexibility, so you still have time for hobbies.

    Working seniors on Social Security who earn more than a certain amount from their jobs are at risk of losing some of their benefits to the earnings test. This withholds $1 from your checks for every $2 you earn over $25,560 in 2027 if you're under your full retirement age (FRA) all year. This is 67 if you were born in 1960 or later. Those who will reach their FRA next year only lose $1 for every $3 they earn over $67,920, and only if they earn that much before their birth month. If you're at or over your FRA for all of 2027, you won't have to worry about the earnings test at all.

    Sources indicate that losses from the earnings test could shrink or even temporarily eliminate your Social Security checks, forcing you to rely more heavily on personal savings and income from your job. You’ll get a one-time benefit boost when you reach your FRA to make up for what you lost to the earnings test in years past, but that won't help you much in the short term. Make sure you have a blueprint for how you'll cover what your benefits won't.

    Sources indicate that if you're on Social Security, your job could force you to owe Social Security benefit taxes, even if you've never faced them before. Or you could pay more in benefit taxes than you're used to. That's because the government looks at your provisional income -- adjusted gross income (AGI), plus nontaxable interest and half of your annual Social Security benefit -- when deciding whether your benefits are taxable.

    According to recent reports, income from a job could increase your AGI, and that could make up to 85% of your benefits taxable at your ordinary income tax rate. This could add hundreds or thousands of dollars to your tax bill. But that doesn't mean you'll have an outstanding balance when you file your return. If you normally get refunds, this might be enough to offset the additional taxes.

    None of these things are reasons to avoid seeking out another job if you really need the income. The money you earn will likely be enough to offset these extra costs. But make sure you're budgeting accordingly, so you don't run into any surprises later.

    #4194. ​Speed And Steering: Make Room For Both In One-On-Ones You Run

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (925 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    ​Speed And Steering: Make Room For Both In One-On-Ones You Run

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (925 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Aditi Khullar, VP at Two Sigma, senior engineer bridging research to production; experience leading AI/ML teams.
    • When my dad taught me to drive in an empty parking lot, he gave me only two pieces of advice: Watch your speed and look where you want to go.
    • The same holds true in engineering management, except the lot is never empty and everyone else is driving, too.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Aditi Khullar, VP at Two Sigma, senior engineer bridging research to production; experience leading AI/ML teams.

    When my dad taught me to drive in an empty parking lot, he gave me only two pieces of advice: Watch your speed and look where you want to go.

    The same holds true in engineering management, except the lot is never empty and everyone else is driving, too. Here, the questions you ask are your biggest tool. They set the team’s speed and the direction of its mission, and they come in two kinds. Momentum questions (how and when) control the speed, moving the work along a path already chosen. Direction questions (what and why) do the steering; they set priorities and, when needed, force a pivot.

    Recent findings suggest that for years, I asked both kinds in the same one-on-one, and I always gravitated toward the momentum questions. My own sense of urgency, and my team’s drive to get things done, kept pulling our conversations toward one more blocker to clear. The direction questions, which could slow things down, kept slipping to next week. So, I split the hour in two: the first half for momentum, the second for direction.

    In a recent development, andy Grove made the case for a full hour decades ago, because the harder topics rarely surface in the first twenty minutes. I recommend you protect a full hour with each report, every week, and give each kind of question its own protected time.

    Industry observers note that the first part of a one-on-one is about the work in front of your team. Follow their lead and keep it moving: what is blocking you, what do you need from me, how will you test it, when will it land. These questions clear the road and, asked consistently, teach people to ask them of themselves.

    They help you as much as it helps them. As Alison Wood Brooks and Leslie John found, questions like these surface risks while they are still easy to fix and give you an honest picture of where the work stands, so you can escalate early and report the status with confidence.

    Speed only helps if you are heading the right way, which is where direction questions come in.

    According to recent reports, this is where you steer, and where you get to know the person you are steering with. As you grow more senior, you earn more license to nudge, direct and, when it matters, drive.

    In a recent development, one engineer wanted to grow into a new role, so I chose projects to build those skills. With another, I was honest about how their pace was being perceived and what it could mean for their trajectory. These conversations build trust, because people see you have their interests at heart. The more often you have them, the fewer hard ones you need, and the easier those land.

    Skip the direction questions, and what drives a person never gets discussed, and their growth is left to whichever project lands on their desk. Protect this time, and you can match people to work that stretches them, so they grow and the project gets their best.

    It is worth noting, however, that some things don’t fit either half. A strained relationship with a teammate, or a hard time outside of work, can matter more than any deadline. When that happens, let the hour make room for it.

    The split matters more than the schedule, and the two parts do not have to run on the same rhythm.

    During a delivery push, momentum may need a weekly beat while direction moves to every other week, and skip-levels and quarterly reviews can carry the bigger direction questions. What matters is that direction has a protected place somewhere, even when it is not every week.

    The balance also shifts with seniority, or what Andy Grove called task-relevant maturity. With junior engineers, the discussion often gravitates to momentum questions, because asking how they will test a change, week after week, is often how they learn to ask it themselves. Senior engineers already ask those questions, so their hour moves toward direction, and too many momentum questions aimed at them could be perceived as micromanagement. Google’s Project Oxygen found the same, with engineers disliking technical micromanagement but welcoming close attention to their careers.

    Recent findings suggest that engineers shift from momentum toward direction as they grow. Teams don’t. They need direction questions at every stage, and only the question changes. A new team needs, “What are we building, and why?” A mature team needs, “Is this still the right thing?” to catch the drift of running on autopilot.

    Sources indicate that whatever the mix, the direction questions are where you learn both where the team is heading and where each person fits in it. So, before your next one-on-one, don’t ask what you need to cover. Ask whether you are there to increase the speed or to change the direction, and give each its own portion of the hour.​.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, it's been a turbulent November for Nvidia (NVDA -3.43%) as the tech giant deals with the unexpected resignation of founder and longtime CEO Jensen Huang.
    • According to recent reports, nevertheless, Nvidia's latest financial results suggest the company's business is expanding at a record pace.
    • According to recent reports, with that said, one financial metric could ultimately drive the stock to upcoming highs: earnings per share (EPS).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Adam Spatacco – Nov 20, 2026 at 8:30AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

    According to recent reports, it's been a turbulent November for Nvidia (NVDA -3.43%) as the tech giant deals with the unexpected resignation of founder and longtime CEO Jensen Huang. Uncertainty surrounding the company's leadership transition, investigations involving ties to China, and questions about its artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure partnerships are weighing heavily on investor sentiment.

    According to recent reports, nevertheless, Nvidia's latest financial results suggest the company's business is expanding at a record pace. During its fiscal third quarter (ended Oct. 25), Nvidia generated $115.8 billion in revenue, representing 103% year-over-year growth. Meanwhile, adjusted earnings per share (EPS) climbed 111% to $2.68. Despite this impressive performance, Nvidia stock is trading roughly 37% below its all-time high.

    According to recent reports, with that said, one financial metric could ultimately drive the stock to upcoming highs: earnings per share (EPS). Nvidia has two opportunities to expand EPS over the coming year, combining organic profit growth with an enormous share repurchase program.

    According to recent reports, nvidia's first opportunity to increase EPS comes directly from its underlying business. The organization is a key beneficiary of AI-driven demand from hyperscalers expanding their data center build-outs. Nvidia's data center division generated $107.6 billion in revenue during the third quarter, increasing 110% year over year.

    Sources indicate that what's particularly impressive is Nvidia's ability to convert its top-line growth into substantial profits. During the third quarter, the organization reported a gross margin of 74.8%. This reflects the pricing power associated with Nvidia's GPUs, networking products, and CUDA software ecosystem. These economics allow Nvidia to generate enormous profits alongside an accelerating revenue base.

    It has been revealed that although management expects gross margin to moderate to between 71% and 72% in the fourth quarter, it anticipates a recovery to between 72% and 73% in fiscal 2028. More importantly, interim CEO Colette Kress raised the company's fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to approximately 75% year over year, up from its previous projection of 70%.

    Even if gross margin remains below its peak, Nvidia can still produce higher earnings through increased sales volumes and operating leverage. In other words, as revenue grows, certain operating expenses may increase at a slower rate relative to sales. This would allow additional revenue to contribute disproportionately to operating profits. The idea here is that Nvidia doesn't necessarily need to maintain record gross margins to achieve record earnings.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:55 AM ET 11/20/26.

    It has been revealed that nvidia's second earnings catalyst is its share repurchase authorization. In September, Nvidia's board of directors approved a $150 billion increase to its existing repurchase program. As of the end of the fiscal third quarter, Nvidia had $227.3 billion remaining under its authorization.

    Management affirmed its intention to execute the remaining portion of the repurchase authorization by the end of fiscal 2028. This makes stock buybacks an notable, albeit underrated, component of Nvidia's capital allocation strategy. The significance of Nvidia's share repurchases becomes clearer once you understand how EPS is calculated.

    According to recent reports, earnings per share equals a firm's net income divided by its shares outstanding. When Nvidia repurchases and retires shares, the company effectively reduces the denominator in that equation. This means EPS can increase even if net income remains unchanged.

    For example, suppose a tech giant generates $100 billion in annual net income across 25 billion shares. That would translate into EPS of $4.00. If the same company reduced its share count by 5%, while net income remained unchanged, EPS would increase to $4.21 without any additional revenue or profit growth.

    Stock prices are influenced by two interconnected variables: earnings per share and the valuation multiple investors are willing to pay for those earnings. A company's share price can rise even when its price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio remains unchanged, provided EPS increases. This unique relationship makes the mechanics around Nvidia's potential earnings expansion particularly interesting.

    Recent findings suggest that nvidia's combination of projected revenue growth, compounding profitability, and aggressive share repurchases creates a compelling outlook around next year's EPS. These catalysts provide the foundation for a bounceback in Nvidia stock even without assuming a dramatic increase in the manufacturer's valuation multiple.

    It has been revealed that I think Nvidia stock could soar next year, driven by accelerating EPS growth rather than speculative enthusiasm. Against this backdrop, investors should monitor Nvidia's net income growth and changes in shares outstanding over the coming quarters. Taken together, these metrics could reveal whether Nvidia's financial performance is strong enough to overcome its recent challenges and propel the stock to upcoming highs.

    Industry News: Cathie Wood's Ark Has Been Selling Palantir Stock. Under $160, I'd Buy It Now.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 10 stocks we like better than Palantir Technologies ›.
    • Recent findings suggest that funds run by Cathie Wood's Ark Invest sold 58,339 shares in Palantir Technologies (PLTR -1.24%) on Nov.
    • The artificial intelligence (AI) software firm's stock has kept dropping since.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Daniel Sparks – Nov 20, 2026 at 8:44AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Palantir Technologies ›.

    Recent findings suggest that funds run by Cathie Wood's Ark Invest sold 58,339 shares in Palantir Technologies (PLTR -1.24%) on Nov. 12, worth about $10 million at the day's close of $171.58. Ark's flagship fund sold 53,547 of the shares, and its internet-focused fund sold the other 4,792.

    The artificial intelligence (AI) software firm's stock has kept dropping since. As I write, Palantir trades near $157, about 9% below where Ark sold and about 25% below its Oct. 9 record close of $209.05.

    Industry observers note that A big growth investor selling into a slide can look like a vote against the stock. But I don't think that particular sale notes much. And the fall since then has sent shares well below the buy price of around $172 I set for Palantir earlier this month.

    According to recent reports, cathie Wood. Image source: Getty Images.

    Ark trades its Palantir stake often, and in both directions. It sold around $9.6 million of the stock in three days from Oct. 19 through Oct. 21. Then on Nov. 3, the day after Palantir's third-quarter results, Ark bought 63,638 shares across five funds, worth around $11.2 million at that day's close of $175.40.

    In a recent development, so, the Nov. 12 sale mostly undid a purchase Ark made just after earnings. Four days later, though, Ark's robotics-focused fund sold around $16 million of the stock. Counting every November trade through Nov. 16, Ark has sold more Palantir shares than it bought this month.

    The stake is still substantial, too. As of Nov. 18, Ark's flagship fund owned around 2.1 million Palantir shares, worth about $325 million, according to Ark's daily holdings file. The flagship fund's 53,547-share sale on Nov. 12 was under 3% of that.

    Recent findings suggest that showing how consistently the firm has topped its own forecasts, Palantir's third-quarter revenue climbed 96% year over year to around $2.31 billion, about 7% above the midpoint of the guidance management gave in August. It had done that twice already this year. First-quarter revenue was around 6% above the guidance midpoint, and second-quarter revenue about 8% above it. And every report brought a higher full-year outlook. Palantir's 2026 revenue guidance began the year at around $7.19 billion. It's now around $8.53 billion, up about 19%, which would mean growth of 91% over 2025.

    The firm also raised its forecast for U.S. commercial revenue (sales to American businesses) to at least $3.56 billion, which would be growth of at least 143%.

    For the last three months of 2026, Palantir sees revenue of about $2.65 billion, up 88% year over year. That would be down from the third quarter's 96% growth. But if Palantir beats its forecast by a similar margin again, fourth-quarter revenue could come in near $2.8 billion, about twice the $1.41 billion it posted a year before.

    Plus, profits are likely to climb faster than sales. Management sees fourth-quarter non-GAAP (adjusted) operating income of about $1.64 billion, over double the $798 million it posted for the same quarter last year.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:57 AM ET 11/20/26.

    Palantir earned $1.43 a share in its past four reported quarters. At roughly $157, this puts the stock's price-to-earnings ratio near 110.

    That's a high price by nearly any standard. But it's far less extreme than it was a few weeks ago. At its Oct. 9 record close, Palantir's price-to-earnings ratio stood near 179, based on the $1.17 per share Palantir earned over the four quarters through June. Some of that decline in the price-to-earnings ratio came from the earnings side, as the third-quarter report raised the manufacturer's trailing earnings per share by about 22%.

    Measured against analysts' consensus estimate for Palantir's 2027 earnings per share, the stock's forward price-to-earnings ratio is around 62.

    In a recent development, sure, a stock at about 110 times earnings needs years of fast profit growth to pay off. And the guided slowdown to 88% revenue growth is a reminder that Palantir's growth will eventually cool. But I think a business that's topped its own forecast three straight quarters makes that bet easier to take.

    Sources indicate that in the end, I don't think Ark's trim tells investors much about where Palantir is going. The organization's own numbers say more, and they still point to fast growth in both revenue and profits.

    Under $160, I'd consider buying Palantir stock now. But I'd add shares in small batches over the coming months, as a stock this volatile could easily dip further first.

    Would Warren Buffett Buy Anthropic? This Is the One Question He'd Have

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (706 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Legendary investor Warren Buffett led Berkshire Hathaway for 60 years, roughly doubling the annual gains of the S&P 500 over that period.
    • Buffett was also known for his folksy investing advice, and his #1 criterion for investing in a stock was whether it has an economic moat or not, his phrase for a sustainable competitive advantage.
    • Anthropic (ANT -5.45%) just completed its IPO, raising more money in its initial public offering than any firm in history at $81.3 billion.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Jeremy Bowman – Nov 20, 2026 at 8:57AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

    Legendary investor Warren Buffett led Berkshire Hathaway for 60 years, roughly doubling the annual gains of the S&P 500 over that period.

    Buffett was also known for his folksy investing advice, and his #1 criterion for investing in a stock was whether it has an economic moat or not, his phrase for a sustainable competitive advantage.

    Anthropic (ANT -5.45%) just completed its IPO, raising more money in its initial public offering than any firm in history at $81.3 billion.

    The AI lab has reported jaw-dropping growth this year, with revenue up 1,200% over its first three quarters. However, Buffett's top concern may be the most notable question investors can ask about Anthropic right now.

    Anthropic has established itself as the leading AI lab, taking market share from rival OpenAI over the last year, and surpassing it in revenue as it's released a series of frontier models and upcoming Claude products that have decimated competing software stocks.

    However, skeptics have argued that the organization lacks a sustainable competitive advantage, that token prices are falling as cheaper models take more of its business, and that it's essentially in an arms race with OpenAI, which could make it difficult for either company to remain consistently profitable.

    It's clear that the market opportunity in AI is massive, but that alone doesn't establish an economic moat; it just makes the stakes that much higher.

    Anthropic believes that its scale and growth have enabled flywheels that constitute sustainable competitive advantages. The first is its "improvement loop," which essentially means that as more people use the product and it gets more feedback, the models improve, which increases both owners and use cases. Google Search benefits from a similar flywheel.

    The second is its “investment loop”, whereby higher growth leads to more revenue to invest in Claude, which leads to better models and more capabilities. Both loops drive improvements in Claude.

    It has been revealed that according to this logic, Anthropic believes size and scale are its main competitive advantages. The firm also sees Claude, or the frontier intelligence behind its AI chatbot technology, as part of its competitive advantage, and that's been demonstrated by Anthropic's ability to overtake OpenAI despite a later start.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:55 AM ET 11/20/26.

    Buffett is a committed value investor and preferred to invest in companies that he knew how to value.

    Anthropic may face as much uncertainty as any other manufacturer in market history. Some expect its blistering growth to fizzle as companies move away from "tokenmaxxing," or maximizing token consumption, and as cheaper models eat into Anthropic's market share. As token prices come down, some investors are ringing alarm bells about the sustainability of generative AI as a business model, as cheaper models built on distillation could put significant pressure on frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI.

    Buffett almost certainly would not buy the Anthropic IPO for the same reason that he passed on stocks like Alphabet and Amazon early in their history, though he later regretted those decisions.

    Anthropic is full of uncertainty, and there's no easy way to predict the organization's cash flow, even a year from now.

    However, just because Anthropic isn't right for Buffett doesn't mean it doesn't belong in your portfolio. Anthropic has enormous upside potential. The company has identified a $40 trillion market opportunity in front of it, and it has a technological lead and a disruptive product that could touch everything from chip design to robotics to drug discovery.

    It has been revealed that anthropic won't become a Berkshire holding anytime soon, but after a moderate gain on its IPO day, the stock still has a lot of room to run. For growth investors, Anthropic is worth getting some exposure to.

    By Neil Patel – Nov 20, 2026 at 9:00AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Invesco QQQ Trust ›.

    Owning exchange-traded funds (ETFs) can be a smart approach to stock market investing. There are an unlimited number of flavors, though, which can be overwhelming. According to ETF Database, the U.S. has more than 3,800 equity-focused ETFs. How can you even begin to narrow down the list?

    It has been revealed that investors should consider crucial variables, such as fees, performance, and exposure. Taking these factors into account, there's an unstoppable ETF that stands out. It's one I'd think about buying today and holding for decades.

    According to recent reports, in the last decade, the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ -0.60%) has rewarded shareholders with a total return of 527% (as of Nov. 16). The S&P 500 index (^GSPC +0.06%), viewed as the preeminent stock market benchmark that represents 80% of the total U.S. market's value, has delivered a total return of 308% over that time. The QQQ wins by a mile in terms of performance.

    It owns the 100 largest non-financial stocks trading on the Nasdaq exchange. Technology stocks rule, which helps explain its impressive track record. And concentration is high, with the top 10 businesses making up 46% of the ETF.

    Industry observers note that the fee is tough to argue with. The Invesco QQQ Trust charges an expense ratio of 0.18%. That's a small price to pay for such stellar gains.

    It looks like an obvious investment vehicle to own compared to what professionals offer. The vast majority of actively managed large-cap funds deliver returns that fall short of the S&P 500 index over long time horizons. But they still charge clients high fees. That's a terrible deal.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:56 AM ET 11/20/26.

    The growing importance of the technology sector has been the most powerful trend shaping the economy and stock market in recent memory. This has played directly to the benefit of this ETF. But there's absolutely no guarantee that the Invesco QQQ Trust will continue crushing the overall market in the future.

    Artificial intelligence (AI) has been a key tailwind. But the technology's financial payout may fail to live up to the hype, which could spur near-term pain as AI stocks face downward pressure.

    If you're staring at a time horizon measured in decades, though, I believe it's a mistake not to be bullish on technology companies. Nobody knows what upcoming industries, businesses, products, and services will be created. But it's reasonable to assume that disruption and innovation will continue. Owning the Invesco QQQ Trust ensures you'll capture tomorrow's winners.

    Position size should still reflect your investment risk tolerance. For aggressive investors, putting 25% of your portfolio in this ETF, provided you don't have overlapping exposure to the same stocks elsewhere, could be the right move.

    • Anthropic's (ANT -5.04%) IPO was one of the most successful in history, with the stock spiking to $111.50 after the IPO price was set at $83 per share.
    • I'm in the same boat and am staying patient by not buying Anthropic shares yet.
    • According to recent reports, anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Keithen Drury – Nov 20, 2026 at 9:01AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

    Anthropic's (ANT -5.04%) IPO was one of the most successful in history, with the stock spiking to $111.50 after the IPO price was set at $83 per share. However, the stock settled down immediately after that and ended the day at $97.17 per share, up 17%. That's a large gain on day one, and investors may be a bit wary about investing in a stock that rose that much in one day.

    I'm in the same boat and am staying patient by not buying Anthropic shares yet. Why? I've got two important reasons that investors should keep in mind.

    According to recent reports, anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. Image source: Getty Images.

    First, I don't know enough about Anthropic's business and how its management team does earnings reports. That could shift my sentiment one way or another, and I won't know anything about that for a few quarters. So, it could be six months or more before I'm comfortable with how Anthropic does its earnings releases.

    On another earnings note, I want to see how Anthropic's revenue growth is trending. There's no debate about how fast Anthropic is growing, as revenue is increasing at a lightning pace. However, it is slowing down.

    In a recent development, during Q3, its revenue totaled $17 billion, up more than 12-fold year over year. In Q2, its revenue totaled $11.6 billion and $4.7 billion in Q1. When you calculate the quarter-over-quarter growth rates, it reveals something interesting. In Q1, Anthropic's quarter-over-quarter growth rate was 132%. In Q2, that figure accelerated to 144%. In Q3, that total fell off a cliff to 47%.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:59 AM ET 11/20/26.

    Industry observers note that that may seem like a reason to panic, and looking at the actual dollar figures provides more color. From Q1 to Q2, Anthropic added $6.82 billion in revenue. From Q2 to Q3, it added $5.41 billion. So, even from a raw revenue standpoint, Anthropic's Q3 was not nearly as successful as its Q2.

    The question is: will that trend continue in Q4, or will there be a great jump in Q4 due to pent-up demand that maybe wasn't met in Q3?

    I have no idea how to answer this question, which is why I think that staying patient here makes a lot of sense.

    History is also on my side, as I've seen plenty of hot IPOs lose their luster over the weeks after going public.

    The pattern of many hot tech IPOs is pretty clear: the stock rises for a while, then comes tumbling down after initial investor demand has been met.

    Wall Street saw this pattern earlier this year with the Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -3.91%) IPO, and I wouldn't be surprised if Anthropic's stock behaves similarly. However, Anthropic does have one item working in its favor: the end of the year.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:58 AM ET 11/20/26.

    Stocks tend to do quite well at the end of the year because portfolio managers are positioning their clients for 2027 and showing which stocks they're in. What better stock to show ownership of than the latest and greatest artificial intelligence stock that hit the market?

    Anthropic checks a lot of boxes, and it could become a popular buy over the next few months. However, I don't know if that fervor will last, and it could dissipate throughout the start of 2027, aligning with the IPO sell-off schedule that companies like SpaceX have experienced.

    Industry observers note that as a result, I think investors are better off staying patient and waiting about six months before buying the stock. I've done that with SpaceX, and I think staying patient with these upcoming IPOs is key to investing success.

    Netflix Stock Is Down 36% and Wall Street Keeps Downgrading It. History Says That's a Mistake.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (638 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By Manali Pradhan, CFA – Nov 20, 2026 at 9:07AM EST.
    • Industry observers note that shares of Netflix (NFLX +0.77%) are down by more than 36% so far in 2026 (as of Nov.
    • It has been revealed that however, the company subsequently introduced paid account sharing and a lower-priced ad-supported subscription tier that allowed the company to sell commercials for the first time.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Manali Pradhan, CFA – Nov 20, 2026 at 9:07AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Netflix ›.

    Industry observers note that shares of Netflix (NFLX +0.77%) are down by more than 36% so far in 2026 (as of Nov. 18), and some on Wall Street have been growing gloomier about its outlook. Among the analysts who have downgraded its stock this year are those at prominent financial institutions such as Wells Fargo, HSBC, and Needham.

    It has been revealed that however, the company subsequently introduced paid account sharing and a lower-priced ad-supported subscription tier that allowed the company to sell commercials for the first time. Netflix's operating margin also increased from 18% in 2022 to 27% in 2024.

    The question now is whether Netflix can continue growing earnings despite its presently weakening viewer engagement.

    There have been other rough spots for Netflix before.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:54 AM ET 11/20/26.

    Sources indicate that those gains took time to materialize. Investors who bought Netflix immediately after the January 2022 downgrades were still in the red a year later. But over the longer term, improving business performance matters more than analyst downgrades.

    It has been revealed that on Sept. 22, HSBC downgraded Netflix from buy to hold and reduced its 12-month price target from $96 to $76, highlighting weaker viewer engagement and growing competition from Alphabet's YouTube. On Oct. 21, Needham also downgraded the stock from buy to hold due to the firm's slowing revenue growth and concerns about its content offerings.

    In the third quarter, Netflix's revenue increased 11.8% year over year to $12.9 billion, while operating income jumped 37% to $4.5 billion. However, its results from Q3 2025 included a $619 million charge stemming from a tax dispute with Brazilian authorities. Excluding the impact of that expense on the 2025 results, operating income would have increased 15% year over year.

    Netflix's revenue growth is also slowing. The company's year-over-year revenue growth rate declined from 16.2% in the first quarter to 11.8% in the third quarter. Netflix expects further moderation in revenue growth to 11.5% in the fourth quarter. Management also reduced its 2026 advertising revenue forecast from $3 billion to $2.7 billion, mainly because some advertising features are taking longer than expected to launch.

    In a recent development, investors should also consider a $2.8 billion payment Netflix received after its proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery fell through. That one-time termination fee increased Netflix's reported net income and operating cash flow in 2026, but did not affect operating income. Hence, Netflix's reported earnings may make the stock appear cheaper than it is relative to its recurring profits.

    According to recent reports, at its Nov. 18 closing price of $59.82, Netflix traded at approximately 15.9 times analysts' expected 2027 earnings of $3.77 per share. This is considerably below Netflix's forward earnings multiples of more than 30 in each of the previous three years. However, buying at that lower valuation will benefit investors only if Netflix can sustain its expected earnings growth.

    It has been revealed that additionally, the organization's existing subscription business continues to generate substantial profits. Netflix expects an operating margin of 31.5% in 2026, up from 29.5% in 2025.

    Industry observers note that hence, I believe that interested long-term investors should buy Netflix gradually at current prices. The company's track record of successful turnarounds demonstrates its ability to adapt, while its current profitability supports further growth.

    • Obviously, when a stock drops 50% while also experiencing surging revenue growth (138% year over year in the third quarter) and raising full-year revenue guidance for several quarters in a row, the question naturally arises: Is this a buying opportunity?
    • Sources indicate that the thing is, Bloom's extraordinary growth has come at an extraordinary cost.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Steven Porrello – Nov 20, 2026 at 9:15AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Bloom Energy ›.

    My, how the tables have turned on Bloom Energy (BE -5.02%), a stock that traded above $340 as recently as this June. Today, Bloom trades at about $172.

    Obviously, when a stock drops 50% while also experiencing surging revenue growth (138% year over year in the third quarter) and raising full-year revenue guidance for several quarters in a row, the question naturally arises: Is this a buying opportunity?

    Honestly, I'm not so sure that it is.

    NYSE · As of 9:57 AM ET 11/20/26.

    Sources indicate that the thing is, Bloom's extraordinary growth has come at an extraordinary cost. Last quarter, it reported $225 million in operating income, yet it also burned through $27 million in operating cash and spent roughly $153 million in capital expenditures. All in all, free cash flow was negative by about $181 million.

    Sources indicate that lucky for Bloom, it has about $2.5 billion in cash and equivalents, so it's not up a creek without a paddle. Still, I believe it's notable to distinguish between a firm that's growing swiftly and one growing profitably. This is especially pertinent for Bloom, whose capital requirements have historically been substantial and whose ability to generate sustainable profits and free cash flow has long been a question.

    It's also key to consider that Bloom stock, even after its 50% decline, still trades at roughly 11 times its projected 2026 revenue -- a sizable valuation for a tech giant whose primary customers, data center developers, could face delays if the enormous investments in AI fail to deliver the returns expected of them.

    Bloom might be trading lower than it was over the summer, but it's not necessarily a bargain. I would continue to treat it as a growth stock with the potential to supply power to data centers, but with plenty of challenges to overcome before that growth translates into profits.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that it's no secret that the AI market has many interlinked relationships among companies that are both competitors and customers, and Anthropic's (ANT -5.04%) initial public offering certainly highlights this.
    • According to recent reports, the tech giant is spending staggering amounts on compute and infrastructure, but the good news for potential investors is it's spreading its purchases across various providers and time frames.
    • Recent findings suggest that the table below demonstrates a breakdown of its major service deals, their time frames, and a rough estimate of each company's revenue share over the deal period.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Lee Samaha – Nov 20, 2026 at 9:20AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

    Sources indicate that it's no secret that the AI market has many interlinked relationships among companies that are both competitors and customers, and Anthropic's (ANT -5.04%) initial public offering certainly highlights this. The manufacturer's $900.9 billion spending commitments include massive infrastructure service agreements with Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -3.91%), Microsoft (MSFT +0.77%), Alphabet (GOOG +3.43%) (GOOGL +3.16%), and Amazon (AMZN +0.51%). Here's what those commitments mean to each company.

    According to recent reports, the tech giant is spending staggering amounts on compute and infrastructure, but the good news for potential investors is it's spreading its purchases across various providers and time frames. About $451 billion of that $900.9 billion is expected to be spent by the end of 2030, with the rest spread between 2031 and 2045.

    Recent findings suggest that the table below demonstrates a breakdown of its major service deals, their time frames, and a rough estimate of each company's revenue share over the deal period. Two points stick out from this data.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:58 AM ET 11/20/26.

    Industry observers note that first, Anthropic’s deal with SpaceX will allow either party to cancel with just 90 days’ notice in the near future. Second, the share of SpaceX’s estimated revenue that will derive from its deal with the AI lab is highly significant for it.

    Data sources: Anthropic SEC filings, *Visible Alpha Wall Street Consensus, author's analysis.

    SpaceX's exposure to Anthropic is arguably more notable than the 10.1% figure implies because it represents a larger share (about 14.7%) of the expected revenue for its “super intelligence” (SI) segment over the period.

    While Anthropic could conceivably cancel the deal early, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk recently said on X that he thinks "the opposite is going to happen." And in an interview at the DealBook summit this month, he said Anthropic "told me that their sort of highest probability outcome is that they would like an incremental 10 gigawatts of compute from SpaceX.".

    If Musk is right, the risk is arguably that SpaceX could be the party that cancels the deal or attempts to negotiate better terms for itself down the road, not least because Musk believes "the value of compute per watt will increase over time, not decrease." If that assumption proves correct, then SpaceX will be better positioned than Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet to profit from the Anthropic IPO.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Ryan Vanzo – Nov 20, 2026 at 9:30AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Lucid Group ›.

    Recent findings suggest that robotaxis have released in a growing number of metro areas across the U.S. While total market penetration remains low, experts are bullish about how rapidly the build-out will proceed.

    A survey of industry insiders conducted by McKinsey states, "While [Level 4, or highly automated] robo-taxis are now available in the first cities in the United States and China, the global rollout of robo-taxis is now expected to become reality at a large scale in 2030.".

    Private autonomous vehicles aren't predicted to arrive at scale until after robotaxi fleets are scaled. up. McKinsey also says: "Overall, experts expect that robo-taxis will be the first commercial application for L4 in mobility -- not privately owned cars. L4 urban pilots for private passenger cars are expected to be pushed out from 2030 to 2032, and fully autonomous trucking is expected to reach viability by 2032, not 2031.".

    In a recent development, note that this survey of experts believes that robotaxis will become a reality at a large scale by 2030. That suggests a mature robotaxi market in the U.S. will be realized over the next three to four years.

    How big could this market become? Tesla (TSLA -0.83%) bull Cathie Wood of ARK Invest expects robotaxis to become an $8 trillion to $10 trillion market globally over the long term. Estimates from Morgan Stanley are more conservative, calling for a $1 trillion global market by 2040. Still, the bank believes the industry will "reach break-even by 2028 and expand significantly over the following years, with approximately 2.5 million robotaxis in service worldwide by 2035.".

    How can investors profit from the rollout? There are two main strategies, each with two promising stocks worth considering.

    NASDAQ · As of 9:55 AM ET 11/20/26.

    Take a look at the market cap of Uber Technologies (UBER +3.35%). The manufacturer's $140 billion valuation is significantly larger than many automakers' stocks. That's true even though the company doesn't manufacture a single vehicle in its ride-hailing fleet.

    It has been revealed that instead of producing cars, Uber operates a software layer that coordinates their use. The company's ride-sharing platform presently holds a dominant market share in the U.S., with impressive margins and rising free cash flow.

    Uber has invested aggressively in the self-driving revolution, taking direct equity stakes in many automakers. But at a high level, the company remains fairly asset-light. The vast majority of ride-share seekers in the U.S. already look to Uber first for a ride. Autonomous vehicles looking to maximize utilization rates will almost certainly add their vehicles to Uber's huge platform.

    Sources indicate that the exception will be Tesla, which plans to operate its own ride-sharing platform. That strategy makes sense given that it has developed its own self-driving technology and can produce its own vehicles at scale.

    If you want to own the software layer of the autonomous vehicle revolution, Uber and Tesla should top your watch list.

    Industry observers note that there's an old saying worth noting: During a gold rush, sell shovels. That way, you'll profit even if the rush only discovers fool's gold.

    What are the shovels of the robotaxi revolution? The vehicles themselves. EV makers Rivian (RIVN -2.35%) and Lucid Group (LCID -0.36%) have positioned themselves accordingly.

    Industry observers note that both companies have already signed deals with Uber to supply tens of thousands of robotaxis. Lucid and Rivian's long-standing tech-first approach finally appears to be paying off, even if total volumes remain low. Some industry insiders believe other robotaxi operators -- including Alphabet's Waymo, which cannot manufacture robotaxis in-house -- will add to the growing corporate-customer lists of Rivian and Lucid.

    Of the four stocks on this list, Rivian and Uber intrigue me most. Uber's valuation is significantly more attractive than Tesla's. The organization has a free cash flow yield of nearly 7.5%. Rivian, meanwhile, has more capital at its disposal than Lucid, with more-mature production capabilities -- a key benefit for robotaxi operators looking to build scale.

    Sources indicate that investors should keep in mind that the robotaxi story won't play out over months. It will likely take years for Rivian, Uber, Lucid, and Tesla to accumulate meaningful revenue from their robotaxi exposure. But with a trillion-dollar opportunity, all four stocks have a clearly defined growth runway in robotaxis.
